answers.question: What is the difference between CrudRepository, PagingAndSortingRepository, and JpaRepository in Spring Data?
answers.shortTitle: CrudRepository vs JpaRepository — the differences

s1_definition.profdef: `CrudRepository` provides basic create/read/update/delete operations (save, findById, findAll, delete, count, existsById). `PagingAndSortingRepository` extends it with pagination and sorting (findAll(Pageable), findAll(Sort)). `JpaRepository` extends PagingAndSortingRepository and adds JPA-specific batch and flush operations (saveAll, flush, saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, getReferenceById) plus List-returning overrides. They form an inheritance chain of increasing capability.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of three tiers of bank-teller training. CrudRepository is the basic teller who can open, read, update, and close accounts one at a time. PagingAndSortingRepository is a teller who can also hand you results "20 at a time, sorted by date." JpaRepository is the senior teller who can additionally do bulk operations efficiently — save a whole stack at once, flush immediately to the vault, or batch-delete — which is exactly what National Bank of India needs for heavy processing.
s1_definition.oneliner: CrudRepository is basic CRUD, PagingAndSortingRepository adds paging/sorting, and JpaRepository adds JPA batch and flush power.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `CrudRepository` provides basic create/read/update/delete operations (save, findById, findAll, delete, count, existsById). `PagingAndSortingRepository` extends it with pagination and sorting (findAll(Pageable), findAll(Sort)). `JpaRepository` extends PagingAndSortingRepository and adds JPA-specific batch and flush operations (saveAll, flush, saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, getReferenceById) plus List-returning overrides. They form an inheritance chain of increasing capability.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of three tiers of bank-teller training. CrudRepository is the basic teller who can open, read, update, and close accounts one at a time. PagingAndSortingRepository is a teller who can also hand you results "20 at a time, sorted by date." JpaRepository is the senior teller who can additionally do bulk operations efficiently — save a whole stack at once, flush immediately to the vault, or batch-delete — which is exactly what National Bank of India needs for heavy processing.

**One line to remember:** CrudRepository is basic CRUD, PagingAndSortingRepository adds paging/sorting, and JpaRepository adds JPA batch and flush power.

sections.s2_technical:
CrudRepository offers the essentials. For example, `repo.save(account)` inserts or updates, `repo.findById("SAV2001")` returns an Optional, `repo.findAll()` returns an Iterable, `repo.deleteById(id)` removes, `repo.count()` and `repo.existsById(id)` give totals and existence checks. Its findAll returns an Iterable, which is less convenient than a List.

PagingAndSortingRepository adds `findAll(Pageable pageable)` returning a Page and `findAll(Sort sort)` returning sorted results. This is where you get the page/size/sort abstraction for large banking result sets.

JpaRepository extends both and adds JPA-flavoured methods. `saveAll(iterable)` persists many entities; `flush()` forces pending changes to the database immediately rather than at commit; `saveAndFlush(entity)` saves and flushes in one call, useful when you need the generated id or trigger side effects now; `deleteAllInBatch()` issues a single bulk DELETE instead of per-row deletes; and `getReferenceById(id)` returns a lazy proxy (formerly getOne). JpaRepository also overrides findAll to return a List, which is more ergonomic.

When to use which: expose the narrowest interface that meets the need. For a simple lookup service, CrudRepository is enough and signals intent. For paginated reads, PagingAndSortingRepository. For batch jobs and flush control, JpaRepository. In practice most teams default to JpaRepository because batch operations and List returns are commonly needed, but exposing CrudRepository can be a cleaner contract when you want to restrict callers to basic operations.

Senior nuances: deleteAllInBatch bypasses cascade and lifecycle callbacks because it is a bulk JPQL delete, so use it carefully where @PreRemove logic or cascades matter. saveAndFlush is often misused — forcing a flush in a loop defeats batching; prefer saveAll plus a single flush. getReferenceById throwing EntityNotFoundException lazily can surprise callers, so prefer findById when you need to confirm existence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A simple customer-lookup micro-service only needs to find and save accounts. Exposing a huge interface would mislead callers. This is exactly CrudRepository — minimal, clear intent.

Problem 2 — A statement screen needs paginated, sorted transactions. This is exactly PagingAndSortingRepository.

Problem 3 — A nightly job imports 100,000 accounts and must bulk-save efficiently and occasionally flush to get generated ids. This is exactly JpaRepository with saveAll, flush, and deleteAllInBatch.

We will build three repositories, each extending the appropriate interface, and a service using them.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
repo-tiers-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/repos/
│   │   │   ├── ReposApplication.java
│   │   │   ├── service/AccountBatchService.java
│   │   │   ├── repository/SimpleAccountRepository.java
│   │   │   ├── repository/PagedTxnRepository.java
│   │   │   ├── repository/BatchAccountRepository.java
│   │   │   ├── model/Account.java
│   │   │   └── model/Txn.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       ├── application.yml
│   │       └── db/migration/V1__repos.sql
│   └── test/java/com/bank/repos/service/AccountBatchServiceTest.java
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -jar target/repo-tiers-service-1.0.0.jar

# Single lookup (CrudRepository)
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001

# Bulk import (JpaRepository saveAll + flush)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/import \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '[{"id":"SAV2001","holderName":"Rajesh Kumar","balance":1000000}]'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: find SAV2001 (Crud); import 1,000 accounts (Jpa saveAll); purge all (Jpa deleteAllInBatch).

Step 1 — find uses SimpleAccountRepository (CrudRepository). It issues one SELECT by primary key and returns the account. The interface exposes only basic operations, so a reviewer immediately knows this service does not do bulk work.

Step 2 — importAccounts uses BatchAccountRepository (JpaRepository). saveAll adds all 1,000 accounts to the persistence context; with hibernate batch_size 500 configured, the inserts are grouped into batches of 500, so instead of 1,000 round-trips there are two batched INSERT statements.

Step 3 — flush is called once at the end, pushing the batched inserts to the database within the transaction. Calling flush per row would have defeated batching, so the single flush is deliberate.

Step 4 — purgeAll uses deleteAllInBatch, which issues a single `DELETE FROM accounts` rather than loading each entity and deleting it one by one. The trade-off is that it bypasses cascade and @PreRemove callbacks, so it is only safe where those are not needed.

```
Hibernate: select ... from accounts where id=?           (Crud findById)
Hibernate: insert into accounts ... (batch of 500) x2     (Jpa saveAll)
INFO  Imported 1000 accounts in batches
Hibernate: delete from accounts                           (deleteAllInBatch)
WARNING  Purged all accounts via deleteAllInBatch
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Operations
    │
    ├─ LOOKUP (CrudRepository)
    │    findById → SELECT by PK → Account
    │
    ├─ BULK IMPORT (JpaRepository)
    │    saveAll(1000) → batched INSERT x2 (batch_size 500)
    │    flush() once → all rows persisted
    │
    └─ BULK DELETE (JpaRepository)
         deleteAllInBatch → single DELETE
         (bypasses cascade + @PreRemove)
    ▼
  DB consistent; batch ops minimize round-trips
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Repository Tiers ═══

  ┌────────┐ REST ┌─────────────┐ REST ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Batch  │─────→│ API Gateway │─────→│ Account Service ×3  │
  │ + API  │      │ JWT         │      │ Crud/Paging/Jpa     │
  └────────┘      └─────────────┘      └─────────┬──────────┘
                           saveAll batched        │ JDBC (batch_size 500)
                                          ┌───────┴──────────┐
                                          ▼                  ▼
                                ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
                                │ PostgreSQL        │ │ batch metrics│
                                │ accounts, txns    │ │ (round-trips)│
                                └──────────────────┘ └──────────────┘
  Narrow interfaces per use case; JpaRepository only where batch needed.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — CrudRepository vs JpaRepository ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Interface Segregation: expose only needed ops       │
  │ Template Method: SimpleJpaRepository implements all  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ I: pick the narrowest repository interface          │
  │ L: JpaRepository substitutable wherever Crud used   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> CrudRepository  │  save, findById, delete, count
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ extends
                 ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ PagingAndSortingRepository    │  + findAll(Pageable/Sort)
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ extends
                 ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> JpaRepository   │  + saveAll, flush, saveAndFlush
  │                               │  + deleteAllInBatch, getReferenceById
  │                               │  + List findAll()
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (import) ──
  1. importAccounts(1000) → saveAll (batched)
  2.   flush() once → INSERT batches
  3. commit
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
These three interfaces form an inheritance chain of increasing capability. CrudRepository provides the essentials: save, findById returning an Optional, findAll returning an Iterable, delete, count, and existsById. PagingAndSortingRepository extends it and adds findAll with a Pageable and findAll with a Sort, which is where I get the page, size, and sort abstraction for large result sets. JpaRepository extends PagingAndSortingRepository and layers on JPA-specific power: saveAll for bulk persistence, flush and saveAndFlush for explicit flush control, deleteAllInBatch for a single bulk delete, getReferenceById for a lazy proxy, and it overrides findAll to return a List instead of an Iterable.

My guiding principle is interface segregation: I expose the narrowest interface that meets the need so the contract communicates intent. A simple customer-lookup service extends CrudRepository so a reviewer immediately knows it does only basic operations. A paginated statement screen extends PagingAndSortingRepository. A batch job that imports or purges large volumes extends JpaRepository because it needs saveAll, flush, and deleteAllInBatch. In practice many teams default to JpaRepository because List returns and batch operations are commonly useful, which is fine, but I still consider whether a narrower interface would be a cleaner contract.

In our National Bank of India system, the lookup micro-service uses CrudRepository, and the nightly import of a hundred thousand accounts uses JpaRepository's saveAll with a configured Hibernate batch size so inserts are grouped into a handful of batched statements rather than a hundred thousand round-trips, followed by a single flush at the end. I deliberately do not flush per row because that would defeat batching.

The senior cautions I always mention are that deleteAllInBatch issues a bulk JPQL delete that bypasses cascades and PreRemove callbacks, so I only use it where that lifecycle logic does not matter, that saveAndFlush is frequently misused inside loops in a way that destroys batching, and that getReferenceById throws its not-found exception lazily, so when I actually need to confirm existence I use findById instead.

answers.question: What is the difference between the Repository pattern and the DAO pattern, and how do they help with abstraction, swappable data stores, and testability?
answers.shortTitle: Repository pattern vs DAO — abstraction, swappable store, testability

s1_definition.profdef: The DAO (Data Access Object) pattern abstracts and encapsulates access to a specific data source, exposing persistence operations typically mapped to a single table or entity, close to the storage mechanism. The Repository pattern, from Domain-Driven Design, is a higher-level abstraction that mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers, presenting a collection-like interface for aggregate roots and expressing domain intent rather than storage detail. Both decouple business logic from persistence, enabling swappable stores and easier testing via mocking.
s1_definition.analogy: A DAO is like a specialist filing clerk at National Bank of India who knows exactly which cabinet, drawer, and folder format holds account records — very close to the physical storage. A Repository is like a librarian who gives you a clean collection view: "give me the account for Rajesh" or "find all overdrawn accounts," without you ever knowing whether the data lives in a filing cabinet, a database, or a cloud store. The librarian speaks the language of the business; the clerk speaks the language of the storage.
s1_definition.oneliner: DAO abstracts the data source table-by-table; Repository abstracts the domain as a collection of aggregates — both hide persistence so the store is swappable and testable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The DAO (Data Access Object) pattern abstracts and encapsulates access to a specific data source, exposing persistence operations typically mapped to a single table or entity, close to the storage mechanism. The Repository pattern, from Domain-Driven Design, is a higher-level abstraction that mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers, presenting a collection-like interface for aggregate roots and expressing domain intent rather than storage detail. Both decouple business logic from persistence, enabling swappable stores and easier testing via mocking.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A DAO is like a specialist filing clerk at National Bank of India who knows exactly which cabinet, drawer, and folder format holds account records — very close to the physical storage. A Repository is like a librarian who gives you a clean collection view: "give me the account for Rajesh" or "find all overdrawn accounts," without you ever knowing whether the data lives in a filing cabinet, a database, or a cloud store. The librarian speaks the language of the business; the clerk speaks the language of the storage.

**One line to remember:** DAO abstracts the data source table-by-table; Repository abstracts the domain as a collection of aggregates — both hide persistence so the store is swappable and testable.

sections.s2_technical:
A DAO typically mirrors a table. For example, an AccountDao exposes `insert(Account)`, `findById(String)`, `update(Account)`, `delete(String)`. It is storage-oriented and often contains SQL or JPA calls directly. You might have one DAO per table and compose them in the service layer.

A Repository is domain-oriented and treats persistence as an in-memory collection of aggregate roots. For example, an AccountRepository exposes `findById`, `save`, and domain-intent queries like `findOverdrawnAccounts()` or `findByHolderPan(pan)`. In Spring Data, extending JpaRepository gives you a Repository whose implementation is generated at runtime; you never write the boilerplate.

Both patterns deliver three benefits. Abstraction: business code depends on an interface, not on JDBC, JPA, or a specific vendor, so a change in storage technology does not ripple into services. Swappable store: because callers depend on the interface, you can provide a JPA implementation today and a MongoDB or in-memory implementation tomorrow without touching the service. Testability: you can mock the repository interface in unit tests, so the service logic is tested without a database.

The practical difference in modern Spring applications: Spring Data Repository is the default because it eliminates boilerplate and expresses domain intent, while a hand-written DAO is still useful when you need fine-grained control over SQL, stored procedures, or a non-JPA data source. Many systems use repositories for the common case and drop to a custom DAO (or a repository custom-implementation fragment) for complex queries.

Senior nuances: a Repository in strict DDD manages whole aggregates and enforces that you load and save an aggregate root as a unit, which protects invariants. A DAO does not carry that domain contract. Also, hiding the store behind an interface is only truly swappable if you avoid leaking store-specific types (like JPA entities with lazy proxies) across the boundary — returning DTOs or domain objects keeps the abstraction honest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Our services call JPA directly, so when we considered moving some reads to a document store, the change touched dozens of service classes. We need the business code to depend on an abstraction, not on the storage. This is exactly what Repository/DAO abstraction provides.

Problem 2 — We want to unit-test the overdraft-detection logic without a real database. This is exactly testability through a mockable interface.

Problem 3 — We want the option to back the same AccountRepository with JPA in production and an in-memory map in tests or a different store later. This is exactly the swappable-store benefit.

We will define an AccountRepository domain interface, a JPA implementation, and an in-memory implementation, plus a service that depends only on the interface.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
repository-pattern-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/repo/
│   │   │   ├── RepoApplication.java
│   │   │   ├── service/OverdraftService.java
│   │   │   ├── domain/AccountRepository.java   (interface)
│   │   │   ├── domain/Account.java             (domain object)
│   │   │   ├── infra/JpaAccountRepository.java
│   │   │   ├── infra/InMemoryAccountRepository.java
│   │   │   └── infra/AccountJpaEntity.java
│   │   └── resources/application.yml
│   └── test/java/com/bank/repo/service/OverdraftServiceTest.java
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run (uses JpaAccountRepository in production)
java -jar target/repository-pattern-service-1.0.0.jar

# List overdrawn accounts
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/overdrawn

# Unit test uses InMemoryAccountRepository — no DB needed
mvn test -Dtest=OverdraftServiceTest
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: find overdrawn accounts; in production CUR3001 has -5,000.

Step 1 — OverdraftService depends only on the AccountRepository interface. Spring injects the JpaAccountRepository in production because it is the @Repository bean.

Step 2 — overdrawnAccounts calls repo.findOverdrawn. The JPA implementation runs a JPQL query over AccountJpaEntity, maps each result to a pure domain Account via toDomain, and returns a list. No JPA entity leaks out of the repository, so the service works only with domain objects.

Step 3 — The service sees CUR3001 as overdrawn (balance -5,000) because the domain Account's isOverdrawn returns true. It logs a warning and returns the list.

Step 4 — In a unit test, we inject InMemoryAccountRepository instead, seed it with a couple of Account objects, and call overdrawnAccounts. The exact same service code runs with zero database involvement, proving testability and a swappable store.

```
Hibernate: select a.* from accounts a where a.balance < 0
WARNING  Found 1 overdrawn accounts
# In test:
WARNING  Found 1 overdrawn accounts   (InMemory, no DB)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  overdrawnAccounts()
    │
    ▼
  OverdraftService  ── depends on AccountRepository (interface)
    │
    ├─ PRODUCTION: JpaAccountRepository
    │    JPQL where balance<0 → map entity→domain Account
    │
    └─ TEST / FUTURE: InMemoryAccountRepository (or MongoDB impl)
         filter map values by isOverdrawn()
    ▼
  List<Account> (pure domain objects, no JPA leak)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Repository Abstraction (swappable store) ═══

  ┌────────┐ REST ┌─────────────┐ REST ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Risk   │─────→│ API Gateway │─────→│ Overdraft Svc ×3    │
  │ Console│      │ JWT         │      │ → AccountRepository  │
  └────────┘      └─────────────┘      └─────────┬──────────┘
                     depends on interface only    │
                              ┌───────────────────┼────────────────┐
                              ▼                    ▼                ▼
                   ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
                   │ JPA impl → PG     │ │ InMemory(test)│ │ Mongo impl   │
                   └──────────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘
  Swap storage by swapping the implementation bean; service unchanged.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Repository vs DAO ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Repository (DDD): collection-like, aggregate root   │
  │ Dependency Inversion: service → interface           │
  │ Adapter: JPA/InMemory adapt store to domain         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ D: OverdraftService depends on AccountRepository     │
  │ L: any impl substitutable (JPA, InMemory, Mongo)     │
  │ S: repository persists; service decides policy       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>> AccountRepository│  findById, save, findOverdrawn
  └───────────────┬────────────────┘
      implements  │
      ┌───────────┼───────────────┐
      ▼           ▼               ▼
  ┌─────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │JpaImpl  │ │InMemoryImpl  │ │MongoImpl │
  │(entity↔ │ │(HashMap)     │ │(future)  │
  │ domain) │ │              │ │          │
  └─────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────┘
        │ used by (DI)
        ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │       OverdraftService        │  no storage knowledge
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. overdrawnAccounts() → repo.findOverdrawn()
  2.   (JPA) JPQL balance<0 → map to domain
  3. return List<Account>
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Both the DAO and Repository patterns exist to decouple business logic from persistence, but they sit at different levels. A DAO abstracts a specific data source and is usually organized table by table, exposing storage-oriented operations like insert, update, and delete, and it tends to live close to the SQL or JPA calls. A Repository, which comes from Domain-Driven Design, is a higher-level abstraction that presents a collection-like view of aggregate roots and speaks the language of the domain, so instead of raw CRUD it exposes intent such as find-overdrawn-accounts or find-by-holder-pan. In Spring Data, extending JpaRepository gives me a Repository whose implementation is generated at runtime, which removes the boilerplate a hand-written DAO would carry.

The three benefits both patterns deliver are abstraction, a swappable store, and testability. Abstraction means my services depend on an interface rather than on JDBC, JPA, or a vendor, so changing storage technology does not ripple through the business code. A swappable store follows directly: because callers depend on the interface, I can back it with JPA in production and an in-memory map in tests, or a document store later, without touching the service. Testability means I can mock or substitute the repository in unit tests and exercise the business logic with no database at all.

In our National Bank of India system I define an AccountRepository domain interface with intent-revealing methods, provide a JPA-backed implementation that maps between the JPA entity and a pure domain object, and provide an in-memory implementation for tests. The overdraft-detection service depends only on the interface, so the exact same service code runs against PostgreSQL in production and against a HashMap in a unit test, which makes the overdraft logic fast and trivial to verify.

The senior nuance I stress is that the abstraction is only genuinely swappable if I do not leak store-specific types across the boundary, so my repository returns domain objects or DTOs rather than JPA entities with lazy proxies. In strict DDD the Repository also manages whole aggregates, loading and saving an aggregate root as a unit to protect its invariants, which is a contract a plain DAO does not carry. In practice I use Spring Data repositories for the common case and drop to a custom implementation fragment or a hand-written DAO only when I need fine control over complex SQL, stored procedures, or a non-JPA source.

answers.question: What are the ways to write custom queries in Spring Data JPA — derived query methods, @Query with JPQL, native SQL, and @Modifying updates?
answers.shortTitle: Custom queries in Spring Data — derived methods, @Query JPQL, native SQL, @Modifying

s1_definition.profdef: Spring Data JPA offers several query mechanisms: derived query methods where the method name is parsed into a query (findByStatusAndBalanceGreaterThan), `@Query` with JPQL for explicit object-oriented queries, `@Query(nativeQuery=true)` for raw SQL when you need database-specific features, and `@Modifying` combined with `@Query` for executing UPDATE and DELETE statements. Each trades convenience against control.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine different ways to ask National Bank of India's system for information. Derived methods are like filling a quick standard form where the field names themselves spell out the request — "find by status and balance greater than." JPQL is writing a short custom request in the bank's internal object language. Native SQL is going straight to the vault's raw filing system when you need a special database trick. And @Modifying is the stamp that says "this request changes records in bulk," like "freeze all dormant accounts in one sweep."
s1_definition.oneliner: Derived methods for simple queries, JPQL for custom object queries, native SQL for database-specific needs, and @Modifying for bulk update/delete.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring Data JPA offers several query mechanisms: derived query methods where the method name is parsed into a query (findByStatusAndBalanceGreaterThan), `@Query` with JPQL for explicit object-oriented queries, `@Query(nativeQuery=true)` for raw SQL when you need database-specific features, and `@Modifying` combined with `@Query` for executing UPDATE and DELETE statements. Each trades convenience against control.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine different ways to ask National Bank of India's system for information. Derived methods are like filling a quick standard form where the field names themselves spell out the request — "find by status and balance greater than." JPQL is writing a short custom request in the bank's internal object language. Native SQL is going straight to the vault's raw filing system when you need a special database trick. And @Modifying is the stamp that says "this request changes records in bulk," like "freeze all dormant accounts in one sweep."

**One line to remember:** Derived methods for simple queries, JPQL for custom object queries, native SQL for database-specific needs, and @Modifying for bulk update/delete.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Support staff search accounts by status and a minimum balance. The condition is simple and the method name reads naturally. This is exactly a derived query method.

Problem 2 — The risk team needs a custom query joining and filtering with full control and a clean method name. This is exactly @Query with JPQL.

Problem 3 — A report needs a PostgreSQL window function that JPQL cannot express. This is exactly a native SQL query.

Problem 4 — A nightly compliance job must freeze every account dormant past a cutoff date in one efficient statement. This is exactly @Modifying with a bulk UPDATE.

We will build an AccountRepository using all four mechanisms.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
custom-query-service/

├── src/

sections.s5_journey:
Input: search ACTIVE accounts above 500,000; freeze accounts dormant before 2025-01-01.

Step 1 — search calls the derived method findByStatusAndBalanceGreaterThan. Spring parsed the name at startup into JPQL `where status = ?1 and balance > ?2` and runs it, returning Rajesh (1,000,000, ACTIVE).

Step 2 — highValue uses the explicit JPQL @Query with named parameters, giving the same kind of result but with an ordering clause and a clean method name.

Step 3 — ranked uses a native SQL query with a PostgreSQL window function rank() over order-by-balance, which JPQL cannot express; the rows map back to Account entities by column name.

Step 4 — freezeDormantBefore calls the @Modifying bulk UPDATE. Because last_activity of CUR3001 is 2024-01-15, which is before the 2025-01-01 cutoff, the single statement `UPDATE accounts SET status='FROZEN' WHERE last_activity < ?` updates that row. clearAutomatically clears the persistence context so any previously loaded CUR3001 entity is not stale.

```
Hibernate: select ... where status=? and balance>?          (derived)
Hibernate: select ... where balance>? and status=? order by balance desc  (JPQL)
Hibernate: select *, rank() over (order by balance desc) ... (native)
Hibernate: update accounts set status='FROZEN' where last_activity<?  (@Modifying)
WARNING  Froze 1 dormant accounts
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring Data JPA gives me four main ways to write queries, and I choose based on complexity and portability. Derived query methods let Spring parse the method name into a query, so findByStatusAndBalanceGreaterThan generates the right JPQL automatically. They are wonderfully readable for simple queries but become unwieldy once the method name carries more than three or four conditions. For anything more complex I use the Query annotation with JPQL, writing the query explicitly against entity names and binding named parameters, which keeps the method name clean and gives me full control over joins, ordering, and projections.

When JPQL cannot express what I need, such as a PostgreSQL window function, common table expression, or array operation, I drop to a native SQL query by setting nativeQuery true. The trade-off is that I lose database portability and JPQL's entity awareness, so I map results carefully by column alias or with a result-set mapping. Finally, Query methods are read-only selects by default, so for bulk updates and deletes I add the Modifying annotation and run the method in a writable transaction; this executes a single bulk statement directly in the database, which is far more efficient than loading and saving thousands of entities.

In our National Bank of India system, support staff search accounts with a readable derived method, the risk team uses explicit JPQL for custom filters, a report uses a native window-function query to rank accounts by balance, and a nightly compliance job uses a Modifying bulk update to freeze every account dormant past a cutoff date in one statement. That bulk freeze would be hopelessly slow if I loaded each dormant account and saved it individually.

The senior cautions I always add are that Modifying bulk operations bypass the persistence context, entity lifecycle callbacks, and cascades, so they can leave stale entities loaded in memory. That is why I set clearAutomatically and flushAutomatically on the Modifying annotation, which flushes pending changes before the bulk statement and clears the context afterward so no stale version of a frozen account lingers. For genuinely dynamic filters where the set of conditions varies at runtime, I move beyond these four mechanisms to the Criteria API or Spring Data Specifications rather than building query strings by hand.

answers.question: What are @QueryHints in JPA, what hints like readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, and timeout control, and how do method-level and transaction-level settings differ?
answers.shortTitle: @QueryHints — readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, timeout at method vs transaction level

s1_definition.profdef: `@QueryHints` attaches JPA/Hibernate query hints to a repository method to tune a specific query's execution. Common hints include `org.hibernate.readOnly` (load entities read-only, skipping dirty-check snapshots), `org.hibernate.cacheable` (use the query cache), `org.hibernate.fetchSize` (JDBC fetch size for streaming large results), and `jakarta.persistence.query.timeout` (abort a query after N milliseconds). Method-level hints apply to one query, whereas transaction-level settings like `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` apply to the whole transaction.
s1_definition.analogy: Query hints are special instructions National Bank of India pins to a single request slip. "readOnly" tells the clerk "I'm only reading, don't bother snapshotting for changes." "cacheable" says "if you fetched this exact list recently, reuse it." "fetchSize" says "bring records to me in bundles of this many instead of all at once or one by one." "timeout" says "if this takes longer than three seconds, give up." Pinning the note to one slip (method level) affects just that request; posting it on the department door (transaction level) affects everything that happens during the whole visit.
s1_definition.oneliner: @QueryHints fine-tune a single query (readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, timeout); @Transactional(readOnly) sets the policy for the whole transaction.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@QueryHints` attaches JPA/Hibernate query hints to a repository method to tune a specific query's execution. Common hints include `org.hibernate.readOnly` (load entities read-only, skipping dirty-check snapshots), `org.hibernate.cacheable` (use the query cache), `org.hibernate.fetchSize` (JDBC fetch size for streaming large results), and `jakarta.persistence.query.timeout` (abort a query after N milliseconds). Method-level hints apply to one query, whereas transaction-level settings like `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` apply to the whole transaction.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Query hints are special instructions National Bank of India pins to a single request slip. "readOnly" tells the clerk "I'm only reading, don't bother snapshotting for changes." "cacheable" says "if you fetched this exact list recently, reuse it." "fetchSize" says "bring records to me in bundles of this many instead of all at once or one by one." "timeout" says "if this takes longer than three seconds, give up." Pinning the note to one slip (method level) affects just that request; posting it on the department door (transaction level) affects everything that happens during the whole visit.

**One line to remember:** @QueryHints fine-tune a single query (readOnly, cacheable, fetchSize, timeout); @Transactional(readOnly) sets the policy for the whole transaction.

sections.s2_technical:
`@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "org.hibernate.readOnly", value = "true"))` on a method loads the returned entities in read-only mode, so Hibernate does not take a dirty-check snapshot and will not flush changes for them. This saves memory and CPU on large read queries even within a writable transaction, and it is more granular than marking the whole transaction read-only.

`org.hibernate.cacheable = true` makes the query use Hibernate's query cache (which must be enabled). For a frequently repeated, rarely changing query like a list of branch codes, the result is cached and reused, avoiding repeated database hits. You pair it with a second-level cache region.

`org.hibernate.fetchSize` sets the JDBC fetch size, controlling how many rows the driver pulls per round trip. For streaming a huge export, a fetch size like 1,000 prevents loading everything into memory at once; combined with a Stream return type and read-only, it enables memory-safe processing of millions of rows.

`jakarta.persistence.query.timeout` (milliseconds) aborts a query that runs too long, protecting the system from a runaway report locking resources. There is also `jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout` for how long to wait for a pessimistic lock.

Method level versus transaction level: a method-level hint affects exactly that query. Transaction-level readOnly affects every query in the transaction, sets the connection read-only, and changes the flush mode. They compose: you might have a writable transaction but mark one heavy reporting query read-only via a hint. The timeout hint on a method bounds that query; a transaction timeout (@Transactional(timeout=...)) bounds the whole transaction.

Senior nuances: the query cache only helps if the underlying entities are also cached and the data is read-mostly; otherwise it adds overhead and invalidation churn. fetchSize behaviour is driver-specific (PostgreSQL needs autocommit off to honour it). readOnly at the method level is a great default for list endpoints because it halves the memory of loaded entities. Always set a query timeout on customer-facing endpoints so a slow query degrades gracefully rather than exhausting the connection pool.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A list endpoint returns thousands of accounts for display only. Tracking them for changes wastes memory. This is exactly the method-level readOnly hint.

Problem 2 — A query for the fixed list of branch codes runs constantly and the data almost never changes. This is exactly the cacheable hint.

Problem 3 — A regulatory export streams millions of transactions and must not load them all into memory. This is exactly the fetchSize hint with streaming.

Problem 4 — A customer-facing search must never hang the thread pool on a slow query. This is exactly the query timeout hint.

We will build a repository whose methods carry the appropriate hints and a service that uses them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: list ACTIVE accounts; fetch branch codes twice; stream all; search by name.

Step 1 — activeList calls listReadOnly carrying the readOnly hint. Hibernate loads the accounts without taking dirty-check snapshots, so they occupy roughly half the memory and will never be flushed as updates. This happens even though the method could be in a writable transaction.

Step 2 — branches calls branchCodesCached with the cacheable hint. The first call runs the SQL and stores the result list in the query cache. The second call within the cache window returns the cached list without touching the database, saving a round trip for this constant, rarely-changing data.

Step 3 — exportCount calls streamAll with fetchSize 1000 and readOnly. The JDBC driver pulls 1,000 rows per round trip instead of materializing millions at once, so memory stays flat while the stream is consumed inside the transaction, then the stream is closed.

Step 4 — search calls searchByName with a 3,000-millisecond timeout hint. If a wildcard search scans too long, the database aborts it and Hibernate throws a QueryTimeoutException rather than tying up the thread and a pooled connection indefinitely.

```
Hibernate: select ... where status=?            (readOnly: no snapshot)
Hibernate: select distinct branch_code ...       (cacheable: first call only)
INFO  branches second call served from query cache (no SQL)
Hibernate: select ... (fetchSize 1000, streamed)
INFO  Streamed 2 accounts for export
Hibernate: select ... where holder_name like ?   (timeout 3000ms)
```

    └─ timeout 3000ms  → abort slow search → QueryTimeoutException

  Method-level hint → one query
  @Transactional(readOnly) → whole transaction policy

  @QueryHint query.timeout → one query

  1. exportCount() [readOnly txn]
  2.   streamAll() fetchSize 1000 → stream open
  3.   consume inside txn → close stream
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Query hints let me tune an individual query's execution without changing what it returns. I attach them with the QueryHints annotation on a repository method. The readOnly hint tells Hibernate to load the returned entities without taking a dirty-check snapshot, which roughly halves their memory footprint and guarantees they are never flushed as updates; this is more granular than a read-only transaction because I can apply it to one heavy query even inside a writable transaction. The cacheable hint routes a query through Hibernate's query cache, which is ideal for constant, rarely-changing lookups like branch codes that are read over and over. The fetchSize hint controls how many rows the JDBC driver pulls per round trip, which is essential for streaming huge result sets so memory stays flat rather than materializing millions of rows at once. The query-timeout hint aborts a query that runs too long, protecting the system from a runaway report.

The method-level versus transaction-level distinction matters. A query hint affects exactly one query, while a transaction-level setting like read-only or timeout on the Transactional annotation applies to every query in the transaction, and read-only additionally sets the connection read-only and changes the flush mode. They compose cleanly: I can run a writable transaction overall yet mark one expensive reporting query read-only through a hint, and I can bound a single query with a query timeout while bounding the whole transaction with a transaction timeout.

In our National Bank of India system, list endpoints that only display data use the method-level readOnly hint to save memory, the branch-code lookup uses the cacheable hint because it is read constantly and almost never changes, the regulatory export streams millions of transactions with a fetch size of a thousand plus read-only so it never blows up the heap, and every customer-facing search carries a three-second query timeout so a slow wildcard search degrades gracefully instead of exhausting the connection pool.

The senior cautions I give are that the query cache only pays off when the underlying entities are also cached and the data is genuinely read-mostly, otherwise invalidation churn makes it a net loss; that fetch size behaviour is driver-specific and PostgreSQL in particular needs autocommit off to honour it, which is why I keep streaming inside a transaction and close the stream; and that setting a query timeout on customer-facing endpoints is not optional in banking, because one slow query without a timeout can cascade into a pool exhaustion outage.

### 9.13 JPA projections three forms (Q36 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: What are the three forms of JPA projections (interface-based, class/DTO constructor, dynamic generic), how does each work, and when do you use which?
answers.shortTitle: JPA projections — interface, class/DTO constructor, dynamic generic form

s1_definition.profdef: A JPA projection returns only the columns an application actually needs instead of the whole entity. Spring Data supports three forms. The first is the INTERFACE projection: you declare a plain Java interface with getter methods (`getFdId()`, `getMaturityAmount()`), Spring Data builds a proxy at runtime that is backed by only those columns. The second is the CLASS/DTO projection: you either write a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new com.bank.dto.FdSummary(f.fdId, f.maturityAmount) FROM FixedDeposit f`, or let Spring Data map directly into a `record`. The third is the DYNAMIC projection: a single repository method declared with a generic type parameter `<T> List<T> findByAccountId(String accountId, Class<T> type)` where the caller passes the projection class at runtime, so the same query can return a lightweight interface, a DTO, or the full entity on demand.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh asks National Bank of India for his fixed-deposit details. The interface projection is a clerk who photocopies only the two lines you asked for onto a slip. The DTO projection is a clerk who hands you a pre-printed receipt with exactly those fields already laid out. The dynamic projection is a clerk who asks "which format would you like today?" and prints whichever one you name at the counter.
s1_definition.oneliner: Interface projection is a proxy over selected getters, DTO/class projection is a `new` constructor expression or record (fastest and most explicit), and dynamic projection takes a `Class<T>` parameter so the caller chooses the shape at runtime.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A JPA projection returns only the columns an application actually needs instead of the whole entity. Spring Data supports three forms. The first is the INTERFACE projection: you declare a plain Java interface with getter methods (`getFdId()`, `getMaturityAmount()`), Spring Data builds a proxy at runtime that is backed by only those columns. The second is the CLASS/DTO projection: you either write a JPQL constructor expression `SELECT new com.bank.dto.FdSummary(f.fdId, f.maturityAmount) FROM FixedDeposit f`, or let Spring Data map directly into a `record`. The third is the DYNAMIC projection: a single repository method declared with a generic type parameter `<T> List<T> findByAccountId(String accountId, Class<T> type)` where the caller passes the projection class at runtime, so the same query can return a lightweight interface, a DTO, or the full entity on demand.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh asks National Bank of India for his fixed-deposit details. The interface projection is a clerk who photocopies only the two lines you asked for onto a slip. The DTO projection is a clerk who hands you a pre-printed receipt with exactly those fields already laid out. The dynamic projection is a clerk who asks "which format would you like today?" and prints whichever one you name at the counter.

**One line to remember:** Interface projection is a proxy over selected getters, DTO/class projection is a `new` constructor expression or record (fastest and most explicit), and dynamic projection takes a `Class<T>` parameter so the caller chooses the shape at runtime.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me set the scene with a real problem from National Bank of India. Our fixed-deposit portal has three screens that all read the same `fixed_deposits` table, and we kept serving them all by loading full entities. That was wasteful and, in one case, dangerous.

Problem 1 — the summary list screen was loading everything. The screen that lists Rajesh's deposits only shows the deposit id and the maturity amount, yet we were loading all twelve columns including the audit fields, and every row entered the persistence context with a dirty-check snapshot. This is exactly where a closed interface projection helps: we declare an interface with just `getFdId()` and `getMaturityAmount()`, and Hibernate fetches only those two columns.

Problem 2 — the API response screen needed a clean, serialisable shape. The detail API returns id, principal, and maturity amount as JSON. Returning the entity risked lazy-proxy serialization issues and leaked internal fields. This is exactly where a DTO constructor projection helps: `SELECT new FdDto(...)` builds a plain record with precisely the three fields the API contract promises, with no proxies to trip over.

Problem 3 — the search screen needed two detail levels from one query. Depending on a toggle, the search either shows a compact row or a full drill-down. We did not want two near-identical finders. This is exactly where a dynamic projection helps: one `<T> findByAccountId(accountId, Class<T>)` method serves the compact interface, the DTO, or the full entity based on what the controller asks for.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `FixedDeposit` entity with twelve columns. There is a closed interface `FdSummary` exposing two getters. There is a `FdDto` record for the API. The `FixedDepositRepository` declares a closed interface finder, a JPQL constructor-expression finder returning `FdDto`, and a dynamic `<T>` finder. The `FdProjectionService` exposes three read methods, each annotated `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, that call the three repository styles and log the column count for each. The `FdProjectionController` exposes the three endpoints. A test verifies the DTO record carries only the chosen fields and that the dynamic method can return different shapes.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a request to list Rajesh's fixed deposits for account `SAV2001`, followed by the API detail call and the dynamic search.

Step 1: The summary call enters `FdProjectionService.summaryByAccount("SAV2001")`, a `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` method, so a read-only Hibernate session is open and no dirty-check snapshots will be taken.

Step 2: The repository returns `List<FdSummary>`. Because `FdSummary` is a closed interface projection, Spring Data narrows the SQL to `SELECT f.fd_id, f.maturity_amount FROM fixed_deposits f WHERE f.account_id = 'SAV2001'`. Only two columns leave the database; the other ten columns including the large `notes` text are never read.

Step 3: Spring Data wraps each row in a lightweight proxy implementing `FdSummary`. These proxies do not enter the persistence context, so there is no snapshot and no dirty checking. The data for `fdId` and `maturityAmount` sits in the proxy; everything else about the row stays in the database.

Step 4: The DTO call runs `findDtoByStatus("ACTIVE")`. The JPQL constructor expression makes Hibernate run `new FdDto(fdId, principal, maturityAmount)` for each row, producing plain records. Three columns are fetched; the records are immutable value objects, safe to serialize to JSON after the session closes.

Step 5: The dynamic call runs `findByAccountId("SAV2001", FdDto.class)`. Spring Data inspects the passed class, sees it is not an entity, and materialises `FdDto` records using the same narrowing it would for a declared DTO finder. Had the caller passed `FixedDeposit.class`, the same method would have returned full managed entities instead.

sections.s6_takeaway:
JPA projections let me fetch only the data a screen actually needs instead of hydrating a full entity, and Spring Data gives me three forms. The interface-based projection is a plain Java interface with getters that match entity properties; Spring Data builds a proxy and, for a closed projection, narrows the SQL to just those columns. The class or DTO projection uses a JPQL constructor expression like SELECT new FdDto with the parameters in the same order as the select clause, or a record return type that Spring Data maps automatically; this is the fastest form because the objects never enter the persistence context, so there is no proxy and no dirty-check snapshot. The dynamic projection declares a single finder with a generic type parameter and a Class argument, so the caller decides at runtime whether to get a lightweight interface, a DTO, or the full entity from one method.

In our fixed-deposit portal at National Bank of India, the summary list uses a closed interface projection that reads only the deposit id and maturity amount, which is two columns instead of twelve. The detail API uses a DTO constructor projection so the JSON contract is explicit and there are no lazy-proxy serialization surprises. The search screen uses a dynamic projection so the same query powers both a compact row and a full drill-down depending on a toggle, without duplicating finders.

The performance ordering I keep in mind is that the DTO projection is fastest because it reads the fewest columns and skips persistence-context management, the closed interface projection is close behind with a small proxy cost, and the full entity is slowest because every row carries a snapshot for dirty checking. The senior cautions are that an open interface projection using a SpEL expression must load the whole entity first and loses the column narrowing, and that nested interface projections across associations can quietly trigger an extra query per row, so I keep projections flat and move to a DTO whenever I need computed or joined values.

### 9.14 Two-table relationship mapping (Q37 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: How do you map a two-table parent-child relationship with @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @JoinColumn and mappedBy, and what does each annotation control?
answers.shortTitle: @OneToMany / @ManyToOne / @JoinColumn / mappedBy — two-table relationship

s1_definition.profdef: In a bidirectional one-to-many relationship there is an OWNING side and an INVERSE side. The child entity (the MANY side) holds `@ManyToOne` plus `@JoinColumn(name = "account_id")`; this is the OWNING side because the child table physically holds the foreign-key column. The parent entity (the ONE side) holds `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account")`; `mappedBy` points at the FIELD NAME on the child that owns the relationship, marking the parent as the INVERSE (non-owning) side. The owning side is what Hibernate reads to decide what to write into the foreign-key column, so you must keep both sides in sync in Java by using helper methods. `@JoinColumn` names the actual FK column; `mappedBy` says "I am not the owner, the foreign key lives over there."
s1_definition.analogy: An account at National Bank of India has many trades. The trades table is where the `account_id` stamp physically lives on each row, so a trade "owns" the link and carries the `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(account_id)`. The account only "knows about" its trades through `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account")` — it is the inverse side, like a customer file that references its receipts but where the actual account number is printed on each receipt, not the other way round.
s1_definition.oneliner: The MANY side with `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn` owns the foreign key; the ONE side with `@OneToMany(mappedBy=...)` is the inverse, and `mappedBy` names the owning field on the child, not a column.

The parent entity (the ONE side) holds `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account")`; `mappedBy` points at the FIELD NAME on the child that owns the relationship, marking the parent as the INVERSE (non-owning) side. The owning side is what Hibernate reads to decide what to write into the foreign-key column, so you must keep both sides in sync in Java by using helper methods. `@JoinColumn` names the actual FK column; `mappedBy` says "I am not the owner, the foreign key lives over there."

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An account at National Bank of India has many trades. The trades table is where the `account_id` stamp physically lives on each row, so a trade "owns" the link and carries the `@ManyToOne @JoinColumn(account_id)`. sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the exact problem we hit at National Bank of India when we first modelled accounts and their trades.

Problem 1 — trades being written with a NULL account. A developer added trades to `account.getTrades()` and called save, but every new row landed with `account_id = NULL`. The screen then showed orphan trades that belonged to no account. This is exactly how the owning side works: the `@OneToMany` collection on the account is the inverse side and does not drive the foreign-key column, so unless the child's `account` field is set, Hibernate has nothing to write into `account_id`. The fix was a synchronisation helper that sets both sides.

Problem 2 — every account lookup dragging in trades we did not want. Because `@ManyToOne` defaults to EAGER on the child, listing trades also eagerly loaded each account, and in some flows the reverse over-fetch happened too. This is exactly where overriding to `FetchType.LAZY` helps: associations load only when explicitly navigated.

Problem 3 — deleting a trade from an account not actually deleting it. Removing a trade from the collection left the database row in place because nothing cascaded. This is exactly where `orphanRemoval = true` helps: a trade removed from its account's collection is treated as an orphan and deleted.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a parent `Account` entity with `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "account", cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true)` and `addTrade`/`removeTrade` helpers that keep both sides in sync. There is a child `Trade` entity with `@ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) @JoinColumn(name = "account_id")`. The `AccountRepository` exposes a `JOIN FETCH` finder so we can load an account with its trades in one query. The `TradingService`, annotated `@Transactional`, opens an account, adds two trades through the helper, saves the parent once, and relies on cascade to insert the children; a second method removes a trade and relies on orphan removal to delete it. The demo proves the foreign key is set correctly, that one save cascades to children, and that removal deletes the orphan row. A test checks the helper sets both sides.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is placing two trades on Rajesh's account `SAV2001`, then cancelling one.

Step 1: `placeTrades("SAV2001")` runs inside a `@Transactional` method, so a Hibernate session is open. It loads the managed `Account` for `SAV2001`.

Step 2: We create two transient `Trade` objects and call `account.addTrade(t1)` and `account.addTrade(t2)`. The helper adds each trade to the account's `trades` list (the inverse side, for navigation) AND sets `trade.setAccount(account)` (the owning side). This second step is what actually matters for the database, because the owning side is what Hibernate reads to fill `account_id`.

Step 3: We call `accountRepo.save(account)` once. Because the relationship has `cascade = CascadeType.ALL`, Hibernate also persists the two new trades. For each, it issues `INSERT INTO trades (trade_id, account_id, symbol, amount, status) VALUES (?, 'SAV2001', ?, ?, ?)`. The `account_id` is `SAV2001` precisely because the owning side was set in the helper — had we skipped that, it would be NULL.

Step 4: The cancel flow loads the account with its trades via `JOIN FETCH` (one query), finds `TRD-001`, and calls `account.removeTrade(trade)`. The helper removes it from the list and sets its `account` to null.

Step 5: On flush, `orphanRemoval = true` sees that `TRD-001` was removed from the owning account's collection and issues `DELETE FROM trades WHERE trade_id = 'TRD-001'`. The row is gone, not merely detached.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In a bidirectional one-to-many relationship there is always an owning side and an inverse side, and the distinction comes straight from the database: the foreign key is a single column on one table. For an account and its trades, the trades table holds the account_id column, so the Trade entity is the owning side and carries the ManyToOne annotation together with JoinColumn naming that foreign-key column. The Account entity is the inverse side and carries OneToMany with mappedBy, and the value of mappedBy is the name of the owning field on the Trade entity, not a column name. The inverse side never drives SQL on its own; Hibernate reads the foreign key only from the owning side.

The classic bug this causes is adding a child only to the parent's collection and forgetting to set the child's reference back to the parent, which leaves the foreign key null. I prevent that with synchronisation helper methods on the parent, like addTrade and removeTrade, that update both the collection and the child's owning reference in one call. In our account and trades model at National Bank of India, those helpers guarantee the account_id is always set, and because the relationship is configured with cascade all and orphan removal, saving the account once inserts all its new trades, and removing a trade from the collection deletes that row.

The production decisions I always make are to override the ManyToOne default from eager to lazy so I do not over-fetch the parent on every child read, to use a JOIN FETCH query when I genuinely need the account with its trades so I avoid the N plus one problem, and to apply cascade only to genuinely owned children. I would cascade from an account to its own trades, but I would never cascade a remove into shared reference data. The senior nuance I mention is that for set-based collections I base equals and hashCode on a stable business key like the trade id rather than the generated primary key, so an entity behaves correctly in the collection both before and after it is assigned a database id.

### 9.15 Composite primary key (Q38 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: How do you model a composite primary key in JPA, and what is the difference between @EmbeddedId and @IdClass?
answers.shortTitle: Composite primary key — @EmbeddedId vs @IdClass

s1_definition.profdef: A composite primary key is a key made of two or more columns together. JPA offers two ways to map it. `@EmbeddedId` uses a single embeddable key class annotated `@Embeddable`, and the entity holds one field of that type annotated `@EmbeddedId`; you access the parts through the key object, for example `statement.getId().getAccountId()`. `@IdClass` keeps the key fields as SEPARATE fields on the entity, each marked `@Id`, and you additionally declare a plain non-entity key class (listed in `@IdClass(...)`) whose field names and types mirror those id fields; the key class exists only so `findById` and the persistence context have a single object to represent the identity. Both require the key class to be `Serializable` and to implement `equals` and `hashCode`. `@EmbeddedId` is more object-oriented and groups the key cleanly; `@IdClass` reads more like plain columns and makes JPQL slightly simpler.
s1_definition.analogy: A monthly account statement at National Bank of India is uniquely identified by the account number PLUS the statement period, together. With `@EmbeddedId` you put those two values inside one little "key envelope" object and the statement carries that envelope. With `@IdClass` you keep the account number and period as two loose fields on the statement and separately describe a matching "key form" so the bank's filing system has one handle for the pair.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@EmbeddedId` embeds one `@Embeddable` key object (access via `getId().getX()`); `@IdClass` keeps separate `@Id` fields on the entity plus a mirror key class — both need `Serializable`, `equals`, and `hashCode`.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the real situation at National Bank of India that forced a composite key.

Problem 1 — a single-column key could not identify a statement. We generate one statement per account per month. Neither the account id alone nor the period alone is unique — Rajesh has twelve statements a year, and October has statements for thousands of accounts. The natural identity is the pair (account id, period) together. This is exactly what a composite primary key models: two columns that are unique only in combination.

Problem 2 — lookups and the identity map kept misbehaving. An early attempt used a generated surrogate id but then had to add a unique constraint on (account id, period) and look statements up by that pair anyway, which meant the surrogate key added nothing. Modelling the real composite identity directly made `findById` natural and made the persistence-context identity map correct — provided the key class implements `equals` and `hashCode` over both fields.

Problem 3 — we needed clean reads for the statement list screen. The screen lists a customer's statements for a year, so queries filter by account id and order by period. With `@EmbeddedId` those queries navigate through the key object, which the team found perfectly readable once the pattern was clear.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `StatementId` class annotated `@Embeddable`, implementing `Serializable`, `equals`, and `hashCode` over `accountId` and `period`. There is a `MonthlyStatement` entity with an `@EmbeddedId StatementId id` plus a `closingBalance`. A `YearMonthConverter` (`AttributeConverter`) stores the period as a `VARCHAR` like `2026-10`. The `StatementRepository` exposes `findById(StatementId)` and a derived finder `findByIdAccountId(String accountId)` that navigates into the embedded key. The `StatementService`, annotated `@Transactional`, creates a statement for (account, period) and reads it back by the composite key. The demo shows that two statements for the same account in different months coexist, and that looking up by the exact pair returns the right one. A test verifies `equals`/`hashCode` on the key.

The input is generating Rajesh's November statement and then reading his October statement back.

Step 1: `generate("SAV2001", "2026-11", 1050000)` builds a `StatementId` from the account id and the parsed `YearMonth`. The key object is the real identity of the row.

Step 2: We construct a `MonthlyStatement` carrying that `@EmbeddedId` and a closing balance, then call `repo.save(statement)`. Step 3: Because the primary key is the pair (account_id, period), this row coexists peacefully with Rajesh's August, September, and October statements — the pair is unique even though neither column is unique alone.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A composite primary key is an identity made of two or more columns that are unique only in combination, and JPA gives me two ways to map it. With EmbeddedId I create one key class annotated Embeddable and the entity holds a single field of that type annotated EmbeddedId, so I access the parts through the key object. With IdClass I keep the key fields as separate fields on the entity, each annotated Id, and I declare a separate mirror class in the IdClass annotation whose field names and types match, so the persistence context has one object to represent the identity. Both styles require the key class to be Serializable, to have a no-arg constructor, and to implement equals and hashCode over all the key fields, because Hibernate uses those methods in its identity map.

In our statement service at National Bank of India, a monthly statement is identified by the account id and the period together, since one account has many monthly statements and one month has statements for many accounts. I modelled that with EmbeddedId: a StatementId embeddable holding the account id and the year-month, and the MonthlyStatement entity carrying it. I look a statement up by constructing the StatementId and passing it to findById, and derived finders navigate into the key, for example findByIdAccountId. I also register an attribute converter so the year-month stores as a clean string column.

I default to EmbeddedId because grouping the key into one immutable value object models the identity as a real concept and reduces mistakes, and I reach for IdClass only when I want the id fields to sit directly on the entity for simpler JPQL or to match a legacy schema. The senior caution I always raise is that a broken equals or hashCode on the key class silently breaks merging and caching, so I implement them over every key field, and I build composite keys from stable business values like an account id and a period that never change, which is exactly the property you want in a primary key.

### 9.16 @ElementCollection vs @OneToMany (Q39 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: What is @ElementCollection, how does it differ from @OneToMany, and when do you use embeddable value objects versus entity relationships?
answers.shortTitle: @ElementCollection vs @OneToMany — value objects vs entity relationships

s1_definition.profdef: `@ElementCollection` maps a collection of BASIC types (like `List<String>`) or `@Embeddable` VALUE objects (like a list of `Nominee` value objects) into a separate collection table that is OWNED by, and has no identity independent of, the owning entity. The elements are NOT entities — they have no `@Id`, no lifecycle of their own, and cannot be queried or loaded on their own. `@CollectionTable(name = ..., joinColumns = ...)` names that table. `@OneToMany`, by contrast, maps a relationship to independent ENTITIES that have their own `@Id`, their own table, their own lifecycle, and can be queried directly. The practical rule: if the child has no identity and only exists as part of its parent (a value), use `@ElementCollection`; if the child is a first-class thing you might query, reference from elsewhere, or manage independently, use `@OneToMany`. A well-known Hibernate caveat: modifying an `@ElementCollection` often triggers a DELETE-ALL-then-REINSERT of the whole collection table, so add an `@OrderColumn` or a primary key to make updates efficient.
s1_definition.analogy: An account at National Bank of India has a list of phone numbers and a list of nominees. Phone numbers are just VALUES — "+91-98765-43210" has no life of its own, you would never look up a phone number as a standalone record. That is `@ElementCollection`. Trades, on the other hand, are real records with their own id that auditors query directly — that is `@OneToMany` to an entity. Values live inside the account's filing folder; entities have their own folders.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@ElementCollection` stores value objects (basics or `@Embeddable`) with no identity in a `@CollectionTable` owned by the parent; `@OneToMany` relates independent entities with their own id and lifecycle — and beware the element-collection delete-all-reinsert without an `@OrderColumn`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@ElementCollection` maps a collection of BASIC types (like `List<String>`) or `@Embeddable` VALUE objects (like a list of `Nominee` value objects) into a separate collection table that is OWNED by, and has no identity independent of, the owning entity. The elements are NOT entities — they have no `@Id`, no lifecycle of their own, and cannot be queried or loaded on their own. `@CollectionTable(name = ..., joinColumns = ...)` names that table. `@OneToMany`, by contrast, maps a relationship to independent ENTITIES that have their own `@Id`, their own table, their own lifecycle, and can be queried directly. The practical rule: if the child has no identity and only exists as part of its parent (a value), use `@ElementCollection`; if the child is a first-class thing you might query, reference from elsewhere, or manage independently, use `@OneToMany`. A well-known Hibernate caveat: modifying an `@ElementCollection` often triggers a DELETE-ALL-then-REINSERT of the whole collection table, so add an `@OrderColumn` or a primary key to make updates efficient.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An account at National Bank of India has a list of phone numbers and a list of nominees. Phone numbers are just VALUES — "+91-98765-43210" has no life of its own, you would never look up a phone number as a standalone record. That is `@ElementCollection`. Trades, on the other hand, are real records with their own id that auditors query directly — that is `@OneToMany` to an entity. Values live inside the account's filing folder; entities have their own folders.

**One line to remember:** `@ElementCollection` stores value objects (basics or `@Embeddable`) with no identity in a `@CollectionTable` owned by the parent; `@OneToMany` relates independent entities with their own id and lifecycle — and beware the element-collection delete-all-reinsert without an `@OrderColumn`.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the modelling decision we faced at National Bank of India for the account profile.

Problem 1 — nominees were wrongly modelled as entities. An early version made `Nominee` a full entity with its own generated id and table. But nobody ever queried a nominee on its own, nominees are never shared between accounts, and a nominee only means something as part of one account. Treating them as entities added a pointless surrogate id and an extra lifecycle to manage. This is exactly what `@ElementCollection` with an `@Embeddable` value object is for: the nominees live in a collection table owned by the account, with no independent identity.

Problem 2 — the phone-number list was over-engineered. Phone numbers are plain strings attached to an account. Making a `Phone` entity for them was overkill. This is exactly what `@ElementCollection` of a basic type handles: a simple `account_phones` table of strings keyed by account.

Problem 3 — trades genuinely needed to be entities. Trades have trade ids, are queried directly by the settlement and audit systems, and have their own status lifecycle. This is exactly where `@OneToMany` to an entity is correct, which contrasts cleanly with the value collections and shows the dividing line.

Problem 4 — early nominee edits were slow and noisy in the SQL log. Updating one nominee deleted and reinserted the whole nominee table for that account. This is exactly the delete-all-reinsert caveat, fixed by adding an `@OrderColumn`.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity with an `@ElementCollection List<String> phoneNumbers` mapped to `account_phones`, an `@ElementCollection List<Nominee> nominees` mapped to `account_nominees` with an `@OrderColumn`, and an `@OneToMany List<Trade> trades` to the `Trade` entity for contrast. `Nominee` is an `@Embeddable` value object with no id. `Trade` is a full entity with its own id. The `AccountService`, annotated `@Transactional`, adds a phone, adds a nominee, and adds a trade, showing that saving the account cascades the value collections automatically while trades are managed as entities. The demo shows the collection tables filling and the ordered update avoiding a full rewrite. A test verifies `Nominee` has no identity and behaves as a value.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is adding a phone number and a nominee to Rajesh's account `SAV2001`.

Step 1: `addPhone("SAV2001", "+91-98765-43210")` runs inside a `@Transactional` method and loads the managed `Account`.

Step 2: We call `account.addPhone(phone)`, adding a plain string to the `phoneNumbers` element collection. We do NOT save a phone separately, because a phone number is a value owned entirely by the account. On flush, Hibernate issues `INSERT INTO account_phones (account_id, phone) VALUES ('SAV2001', '+91-98765-43210')`. The phone has no id of its own; its "identity" is simply that it belongs to `SAV2001`.

Step 3: `addNominee(...)` loads the account and calls `account.addNominee(new Nominee(...))`, appending an embeddable value object to the `nominees` element collection. Because the collection has an `@OrderColumn`, each nominee gets a `position`. On flush, Hibernate issues `INSERT INTO account_nominees (account_id, position, name, relationship, share_percent) VALUES ('SAV2001', 0, 'Asha Kumar', 'SPOUSE', 60)`.

Step 4: The `@OrderColumn` matters for later edits. If we change one nominee, Hibernate can target that specific position row rather than deleting every nominee for the account and reinserting them all — the classic element-collection trap, avoided here.

Step 5: Contrast with trades. A trade is an entity with its own id in the `trades` table, so it is managed independently and can be queried directly by the audit system. The `view` method maps the account, its value collections, and its trade count into a plain `ProfileView` record for JSON.

sections.s6_takeaway:
ElementCollection maps a collection of basic types or embeddable value objects into a separate collection table that is fully owned by the parent entity. The elements have no identity of their own, no primary key, and no independent lifecycle; they are loaded and saved as part of the parent, and I name their table with CollectionTable. OneToMany is completely different: it relates the parent to independent entities that each have their own id, their own table, and their own lifecycle, and which can be queried directly and referenced from elsewhere. The decision rule I apply is to ask whether the child has an identity and whether anyone would ever load or query it on its own. If yes, it is an entity and I use OneToMany; if it is just descriptive data owned by one parent and never shared, it is a value object and I use ElementCollection.

In our account profile at National Bank of India, phone numbers are a collection of plain strings and nominees are embeddable value objects, so both are ElementCollections owned by the account with no independent identity, whereas trades have trade ids, are queried directly by the settlement and audit systems, and have their own status lifecycle, so they are entities mapped with OneToMany. That contrast is the whole point: nominees live inside the account's collection tables, trades have their own table and their own existence.

The senior caution I always raise is the delete-all-reinsert behaviour of element collections. Without an order column or an effective key, Hibernate cannot identify individual rows, so any change to the collection deletes every row for that parent and reinserts the whole thing, which is a real performance trap on large collections. I fix it by adding an OrderColumn so each element has a position and Hibernate can target individual rows. I also remember that value objects cannot be shared between parents, so the moment I want to share a child between two accounts, that child is really an entity and belongs in a proper entity relationship rather than an element collection.
