sections.s6_takeaway:
Migrating a JPA application from MySQL to Oracle touches four layers. First the dialect: I change Hibernate's dialect to the Oracle dialect so it generates Oracle-flavoured SQL, which affects pagination, where MySQL's LIMIT becomes Oracle's FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY, and it affects how Hibernate requests identifiers. Second the driver and URL: I swap the MySQL Connector/J dependency and the jdbc:mysql URL for the Oracle thin driver and a jdbc:oracle:thin URL on port 1521 with the service name. Third, and this is the biggest code change, identifier generation: MySQL auto-increment with GenerationType.IDENTITY does not exist in Oracle the same way, so I switch to GenerationType.SEQUENCE with a sequence generator and create the Oracle sequence, which as a bonus lets Hibernate pre-allocate id blocks and batch inserts, something IDENTITY never allowed. Fourth, schema and type differences: VARCHAR becomes VARCHAR2, DECIMAL becomes NUMBER with precision and scale for money, older Oracle has no native boolean so a Java boolean maps to NUMBER(1) through a converter, large text becomes CLOB, and crucially Oracle treats an empty string as null.

In our core ledger migration at National Bank of India, the account and transaction tables moved from auto-increment keys to Oracle sequences, which also gave us insert batching we never had on MySQL, and the money columns moved from DECIMAL to NUMBER while staying BigDecimal in Java so the mapping was correct on both. We mapped the active flag through a boolean-to-number converter and the notes field to a CLOB.

The senior point I always stress is that the dialect only fixes Hibernate's generated SQL, not any native SQL the team wrote by hand. So before flipping the dialect I audit every native query for MySQL-only constructs like LIMIT or MySQL-specific functions and rewrite them, I audit any code that relied on an empty string being distinct from null because Oracle collapses the two, and I keep identifier naming consistent because Oracle folds unquoted names to uppercase and is case-sensitive for quoted ones. I run the migration in stages with ddl-auto set to validate against a real Oracle instance and a full regression pass, because correctness across the whole application is what the migration must guarantee, not just that the generated SQL compiles.

### 9.25 Large dataset in @Scheduled (Q48 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: How do you process a very large dataset inside a @Scheduled job without running out of memory, blocking too long, overloading the database, or losing progress on errors?
answers.shortTitle: Processing a large dataset in a @Scheduled job — memory, long execution, DB load, error handling

s1_definition.profdef: A scheduled job that loads millions of rows at once risks four problems. MEMORY: `findAll()` into a `List` materialises every row and entity in the heap, causing `OutOfMemoryError`; the fix is to process in CHUNKS/PAGES (keyset pagination or a `Stream`) and flush+clear the persistence context per chunk so entities are garbage-collected. LONG EXECUTION: a single-threaded loop over millions of rows may run for hours and overlap the next scheduled trigger; the fix is to bound the work per run, commit per chunk, and make the job idempotent and resumable. DB LOAD: hammering the database with unbounded queries or huge `IN` clauses starves other traffic; the fix is batched reads/writes, a sensible fetch size, throttling, and running off-peak against a replica where possible. ERRORS: an exception midway can abort the whole job and lose progress; the fix is per-chunk transactions so completed chunks stay committed, recording a cursor/checkpoint, skipping-and-logging poison records, and alerting. In Spring the robust pattern is chunk-oriented processing (Spring Batch) or a hand-written paged loop with per-chunk transactions.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must recalculate interest on ten million accounts every night. Trying to pull all ten million files onto one desk at once collapses the desk (out of memory). The fix is to work through them a tray of five hundred at a time, finishing and filing each tray before fetching the next (chunking), stamping a bookmark after each tray so a crash can resume (checkpoint), not overwhelming the archive clerk with requests (throttling the database), and setting aside any unreadable file to review later instead of abandoning the whole night's work (skip-and-log).
s1_definition.oneliner: For a huge scheduled job, process in chunks with per-chunk transactions and flush+clear the persistence context, bound the work and make it idempotent/resumable via a checkpoint, throttle database load, and skip-and-log bad records instead of aborting — or use Spring Batch's chunk-oriented model.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the nightly interest-accrual job at National Bank of India that this pattern rescued.

Problem 1 — the job ran out of memory. The first version called `accountRepo.findAll()` to load every savings account and crashed with `OutOfMemoryError` once the bank grew past a few hundred thousand accounts. This is exactly the memory problem: loading all rows and entities at once. The fix is keyset-paged chunks with flush+clear per chunk.

Problem 2 — a failure near the end wasted the whole run. The job ran in one big transaction, and an exception on one corrupt account rolled back millions of already-computed accruals. This is exactly the error problem: per-chunk transactions keep completed chunks committed, and skip-and-log handles the one bad record without aborting.

Problem 3 — the job overloaded the database and slowed morning banking. It read and wrote as fast as possible and saturated the primary database. This is exactly the DB-load problem: bounded chunk sizes, batched writes, and a small throttle pause keep the job from starving live traffic.

Problem 4 — restarts started from scratch. When the job was restarted after a crash, it reprocessed everything. This is exactly the long-execution/resumability problem: a checkpoint cursor lets the job resume from the last committed chunk, and idempotent updates make re-running a chunk safe.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity. The `InterestAccrualJob` has a `@Scheduled` method that delegates to the service. The `InterestAccrualService` processes accounts in KEYSET-PAGED chunks of five hundred, each chunk in its own `@Transactional` method that recalculates interest, flushes and clears the persistence context, records a checkpoint cursor, throttles briefly between chunks, and skips-and-logs any poison record. A `JobCheckpoint` entity stores the last processed cursor so a restart resumes. A test verifies the chunking advances the cursor and that a poison record is skipped rather than aborting the chunk. The code notes Spring Batch as the production-grade alternative.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the nightly interest-accrual run over all savings accounts.

Step 1 — entry and checkpoint. At 01:00 the `@Scheduled` method fires and delegates to `service.run()`. The service reads the checkpoint cursor for the job; on a fresh run it is empty, and on a restart after a crash it holds the last committed account id, so processing resumes from there rather than from the start.

Step 2 — bounded chunk read. The service reads the next chunk with keyset pagination: `SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.accountId > :cursor ORDER BY a.accountId` limited to five hundred rows. This bounds both memory (only five hundred entities in the heap) and database load (a small indexed read), and because it is keyset rather than offset, deep chunks stay fast.

Step 3 — per-chunk transaction and processing. `processChunk` runs in its own `@Transactional` method. For each account it computes the idempotent daily accrual (setting, not adding, today's value, so re-running the chunk after a restart produces the same result). If one account throws, the service skips-and-logs it and continues rather than aborting the chunk.

Step 4 — flush, clear, commit. After processing the chunk, the service calls `flush` to write the updates and `clear` to detach the five hundred entities so they can be garbage-collected, preventing the persistence context from growing unbounded. The chunk transaction commits, so this chunk's work is now durable regardless of what happens later.

Step 5 — checkpoint and throttle. The service advances the checkpoint cursor to the last account id in the chunk and commits that too, so a crash now resumes from this point. It then sleeps briefly to avoid saturating the database, and loops to the next chunk. When a read returns fewer than five hundred rows the set is exhausted; the service resets the cursor for next night and logs the totals, including how many poison records were skipped.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Processing a very large dataset in a scheduled job has four risks, and I address each deliberately. The first is memory: loading everything with findAll into a list materialises every row and entity in the heap and causes an out-of-memory error, so I process in bounded chunks using keyset pagination or a stream, and after each chunk I flush and clear the persistence context so the processed entities detach and get garbage-collected. The second is long execution: a single run over millions of rows can last hours and overlap the next trigger, so I bound the work, commit per chunk so progress is durable, and prevent overlapping runs. The third is database load: unbounded queries and tight loops starve live traffic, so I use bounded chunk reads, batched writes, a small throttle between chunks, and I run off-peak or against a replica. The fourth, and most important for correctness, is error handling: if the job runs as one giant transaction and fails near the end, everything rolls back, so I use per-chunk transactions, record a checkpoint cursor so a restart resumes where it stopped, make the updates idempotent so re-running a chunk is safe, and skip-and-log individual poison records instead of aborting.

In our nightly interest-accrual job at National Bank of India, the first version called findAll and crashed with out-of-memory once we grew past a few hundred thousand accounts, and a failure near the end once rolled back millions of computed accruals. We rebuilt it to process five hundred accounts per keyset-paged chunk, each chunk in its own transaction with a flush and clear afterwards, advancing a checkpoint cursor so a crash resumes from the last committed chunk, throttling briefly between chunks so morning banking is not slowed, and skipping-and-logging the occasional corrupt account rather than failing the whole run. The daily accrual is idempotent because it sets rather than adds today's value, so re-running a chunk never double-counts.

The senior recommendation I always add is that for genuinely large, restartable, auditable batch work the production-grade answer is Spring Batch, which gives chunk-oriented processing, a job repository that persists progress, restartability, skip and retry policies, and metrics out of the box. A hand-written paged loop with per-chunk transactions is fine for moderate volumes, but Spring Batch is what I reach for when the dataset is huge and the job must be resumable and observable.

### 9.26 Retry logic in Spring schedulers (Q49 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: How do you add retry logic to a Spring scheduled job using @Retryable and @Recover, and how do backoff, retry-for, max-attempts, and the recover method work?
answers.shortTitle: Retry logic in Spring schedulers — @Retryable and @Recover

s1_definition.profdef: Spring Retry (`spring-retry`) adds declarative retry to a method. `@Retryable` wraps a method so that if it throws a configured exception, Spring re-invokes it up to `maxAttempts` times. `retryFor` (formerly `include`) lists which exception types trigger a retry (for example transient `TransientDataAccessException`), while `noRetryFor` excludes types that should fail fast (for example a validation error that will never succeed on retry). `backoff = @Backoff(delay = ..., multiplier = ..., maxDelay = ...)` spaces out the attempts — a fixed delay or exponential backoff so you do not hammer a struggling dependency. `@Recover` designates a FALLBACK method that Spring calls when all retries are exhausted; its first parameter is the exception type and the remaining parameters match the original method's arguments, letting you log, alert, or write to a dead-letter store. You enable the feature with `@EnableRetry`. In a scheduled job, you apply `@Retryable` to the unit of work (for example per-chunk processing) so transient failures self-heal without failing the whole run.
s1_definition.analogy: When National Bank of India's nightly job calls an external rate service and it briefly times out, `@Retryable` is like the clerk trying the phone again a few times with a growing pause between calls (backoff) instead of giving up at once. `retryFor` says "only redial for a busy signal, not for a wrong number" (retry transient errors, fail fast on permanent ones). `@Recover` is the standing instruction for when all redials fail: "log it, raise a ticket, and move on" rather than abandoning the whole night's work.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@Retryable(retryFor=..., maxAttempts=..., backoff=@Backoff(delay, multiplier))` re-invokes a method on transient failures with spacing, `noRetryFor` fails fast on permanent errors, and `@Recover` is the matching fallback when retries are exhausted — enabled by `@EnableRetry`.
s1_definition.raw:

You enable the feature with `@EnableRetry`. In a scheduled job, you apply `@Retryable` to the unit of work (for example per-chunk processing) so transient failures self-heal without failing the whole run.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When National Bank of India's nightly job calls an external rate service and it briefly times out, `@Retryable` is like the clerk trying the phone again a few times with a growing pause between calls (backoff) instead of giving up at once. `retryFor` says "only redial for a busy signal, not for a wrong number" (retry transient errors, fail fast on permanent ones). `@Recover` is the standing instruction for when all redials fail: "log it, raise a ticket, and move on" rather than abandoning the whole night's work.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the flaky dependency that made retry essential in a scheduled job at National Bank of India.

Problem 1 — a nightly FX-rate sync failed on brief network blips. The job calls an external foreign-exchange rate service to refresh conversion rates. The service occasionally timed out for a second or two, and the whole nightly job failed because of one transient blip. This is exactly where `@Retryable` with exponential backoff helps: the call retries a few times with growing pauses and usually succeeds on the second attempt.

Problem 2 — the job wasted time retrying permanent errors. An early version retried every exception, including a validation error when the request payload was malformed, which could never succeed. This is exactly where `noRetryFor` helps: permanent errors fail fast instead of burning through retries.

Problem 3 — when the rate service was down for the whole window, the job needed a graceful fallback. After exhausting retries, simply throwing left the rates stale with no record. This is exactly where `@Recover` helps: the fallback logs the failure, records it in a failure table for the operations team, and lets the rest of the job continue using the last known good rates.

Problem 4 — retries must not double-apply rates. A retry might fire after a partial success. This is exactly the idempotency requirement: the rate update sets the value for a currency and date, so re-running is safe.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `FxRateService` whose `syncRates` method is `@Retryable` for transient exceptions with exponential backoff and `noRetryFor` on a permanent validation exception, plus a matching `@Recover` fallback that records the failure. A `FlakyRateClient` simulates a dependency that fails a couple of times then succeeds, and can also throw a permanent error. An `FxRate` entity stores rates idempotently by currency and date. The `RateSyncJob` has a `@Scheduled` method that invokes the retryable service. A test verifies that a transient failure is retried and eventually succeeds, that a permanent failure is not retried, and that the recover method runs after exhaustion.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the nightly FX-rate sync, with the rate service briefly flaky for USD and permanently rejecting a bad currency code.

Step 1 — entry. At 00:30 the `@Scheduled` method iterates the currencies and calls `fxRateService.syncRate(currency)` for each. Because the retry is applied per currency, a problem with one does not abort the others.

Step 2 — first attempt fails transiently. For USD, `syncRate` calls the rate client, which throws a `ResourceAccessException` (a timeout). Because this type is in `retryFor`, Spring Retry catches it, waits the initial backoff of 500ms, and re-invokes the method. The method is `@Transactional`, so the failed attempt's transaction rolled back before the retry.

Step 3 — second attempt, longer backoff. The second call also times out. Spring waits 1000ms (500ms times the multiplier of 2) and retries again. The backoff grows exponentially, giving the struggling service room to recover rather than being hammered.

Step 4 — third attempt succeeds. The third call returns a rate. The method saves it with an idempotent upsert keyed by currency and date, so even if an earlier attempt had partially written, re-running is safe. The retry sequence ends successfully and the value is returned.

Step 5 — permanent error fails fast. For a bad currency code, the strict method calls a client that throws `PermanentRateException`. Because that type is in `noRetryFor`, Spring does NOT retry; it fails immediately, saving the time that futile retries would waste.

Step 6 — exhaustion triggers recover. Suppose the rate service is down for the whole window and USD keeps timing out through all four attempts. After the last attempt, Spring looks for a `@Recover` method whose first parameter matches `ResourceAccessException` and whose remaining parameters match the original arguments, and calls `recoverSyncRate(ex, "USD")`. That fallback logs the failure, records it in the `sync_failures` table for operations, and returns without rethrowing, so the job continues with the last known good rates for the other currencies.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring Retry adds declarative retry to a method through the Retryable annotation, enabled by EnableRetry. I list the exception types that should trigger a retry in retryFor, typically transient faults like timeouts or connection resets, and I list the types that should fail fast in noRetryFor, typically permanent faults like a validation error that will never succeed on retry. The maxAttempts attribute counts the initial try plus the retries, so four attempts means one try and three retries. The Backoff annotation spaces the attempts out, with an initial delay, a multiplier that makes the backoff exponential, a maximum delay cap, and optional jitter, which gives a struggling dependency room to recover instead of being hammered. When all attempts are exhausted, Spring calls the Recover method whose first parameter matches the exception and whose remaining parameters match the original method's arguments, so I can log, alert, write to a dead-letter store, and let the rest of the job continue.

In our nightly FX-rate sync at National Bank of India, the external rate service occasionally times out for a second or two, and without retry the whole job failed on a single blip. I made the per-currency sync retryable for the transient timeout exception with exponential backoff starting at five hundred milliseconds and doubling, so it usually succeeds on the second or third attempt, and I put the permanent invalid-currency exception in noRetryFor so it fails fast instead of wasting retries. When the rate service is down for the whole window, the recover method records the failure in a table for operations and returns without rethrowing, so the job continues using the last known good rates. The rate upsert is keyed by currency and date so re-running after a retry never double-applies.

The senior points I always add are that Spring Retry works through an AOP proxy just like transactions, so the retryable method must be called from another bean and not through self-invocation; that each retry of a transactional method should get a fresh transaction because the failed attempt must roll back first; that the operation must be idempotent because an attempt might have partially succeeded; and that for distributed or cross-process retries I prefer a durable mechanism like a message queue with redelivery or Spring Batch's retry and skip policies over in-memory Retryable, because an in-memory retry is lost if the process dies.

### 9.27 @Scheduled runs on every instance (Q50 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: When you run multiple instances of a Spring Boot app, a @Scheduled job fires on EVERY instance. How do you ensure it runs only once, using ShedLock, leader election, or Quartz clustering?
answers.shortTitle: @Scheduled runs on every instance — ShedLock, leader election, Quartz clustering

s1_definition.profdef: A `@Scheduled` task is local to each JVM, so when you run N replicas of a service, each replica fires the job at the trigger time — the job runs N times, which for a banking job (interest accrual, statement generation) can double-charge or duplicate work. Three standard fixes. (1) SHEDLOCK: a lightweight library that wraps a scheduled method with `@SchedulerLock`; before running, each instance tries to acquire a named lock in a shared store (a database table, Redis, etc.); only the one that acquires it runs, the rest skip. The lock has a `lockAtMostFor` (safety timeout so a crashed holder's lock is released) and `lockAtLeastFor` (minimum hold to prevent rapid re-runs). (2) LEADER ELECTION: one instance is elected leader (via ZooKeeper, Spring Cloud, Kubernetes lease, etc.) and only the leader runs scheduled jobs. (3) QUARTZ CLUSTERING: use the Quartz scheduler in clustered mode backed by a shared database (`JDBCJobStore`); Quartz coordinates so each trigger fires on exactly one node, and it persists jobs and supports misfire handling. ShedLock is the simplest for "run once" semantics; Quartz is the richest (persistence, misfire, complex schedules); leader election fits when one node should own ALL periodic work.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs four copies of its batch service for availability. At midnight all four try to generate statements, so every customer gets four statements. ShedLock is like a single shared sign-in sheet at the vault: whoever grabs the pen first does the job, the others see it is taken and walk away. Leader election is like appointing one branch as head office for all nightly tasks. Quartz clustering is like a central scheduling office with a shared diary that assigns each task to exactly one branch and remembers missed appointments.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multiple instances each fire `@Scheduled`, so guard it: ShedLock acquires a named lock in a shared store (`lockAtMostFor`/`lockAtLeastFor`) so only one instance runs; leader election lets only the leader run jobs; Quartz clustering with a shared JDBC store assigns each trigger to exactly one node with persistence and misfire handling.

(2) LEADER ELECTION: one instance is elected leader (via ZooKeeper, Spring Cloud, Kubernetes lease, etc.) and only the leader runs scheduled jobs. (3) QUARTZ CLUSTERING: use the Quartz scheduler in clustered mode backed by a shared database (`JDBCJobStore`); Quartz coordinates so each trigger fires on exactly one node, and it persists jobs and supports misfire handling. ShedLock is the simplest for "run once" semantics; Quartz is the richest (persistence, misfire, complex schedules); leader election fits when one node should own ALL periodic work.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India runs four copies of its batch service for availability. At midnight all four try to generate statements, so every customer gets four statements. ShedLock is like a single shared sign-in sheet at the vault: whoever grabs the pen first does the job, the others see it is taken and walk away. Leader election is like appointing one branch as head office for all nightly tasks. Quartz clustering is like a central scheduling office with a shared diary that assigns each task to exactly one branch and remembers missed appointments.

**One line to remember:** Multiple instances each fire `@Scheduled`, so guard it: ShedLock acquires a named lock in a shared store (`lockAtMostFor`/`lockAtLeastFor`) so only one instance runs; leader election lets only the leader run jobs; Quartz clustering with a shared JDBC store assigns each trigger to exactly one node with persistence and misfire handling.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me explain why the problem happens and then each fix, the way I would when a team moves a scheduled job from one instance to a horizontally-scaled deployment.

The root cause: `@Scheduled` is per-JVM. Spring's scheduler lives inside each application instance and knows nothing about other instances. So with four replicas, the midnight cron fires four times — once per replica. For an idempotent read it is merely wasteful; for a job that writes (accrues interest, generates statements, sends emails) it duplicates financial effects. This is unacceptable in banking.

SHEDLOCK is the lightest fix and my default for simple "run once across the cluster" needs. I add the ShedLock dependency, point it at a shared `LockProvider` (commonly a `shedlock` table in the same database), enable it with `@EnableSchedulerLock`, and annotate the scheduled method with `@SchedulerLock`.

```java
@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 0 * * *")
@SchedulerLock(name = "nightlyStatements",
               lockAtMostFor = "PT30M",   // safety: auto-release after 30 min if the holder crashes
               lockAtLeastFor = "PT5M")   // hold at least 5 min to prevent a fast second run
public void generateStatements() { /* runs on exactly ONE instance */ }
```

How it works: at the trigger, every instance tries to INSERT/UPDATE a row named `nightlyStatements` in the shared lock table. The database's atomicity ensures only one wins; the winner runs the job, the losers find the lock held and skip. `lockAtMostFor` is critical — if the winning instance crashes mid-job, the lock would otherwise be held forever, so it auto-expires after that duration. `lockAtLeastFor` prevents a job that finishes in milliseconds from being re-run by another instance within the same trigger window due to clock skew. ShedLock guarantees "at most once" per trigger; it does NOT provide retry or persistence of the job itself.

LEADER ELECTION designates a single instance as the leader; only the leader executes scheduled jobs, and if it dies another instance takes over. The election backend can be ZooKeeper, Spring Cloud (Consul/ZooKeeper), or a Kubernetes lease. In the scheduled method I check `if (leaderContext.isLeader())` before doing work, or I start/stop the scheduler based on leadership. This suits the case where ONE node should own all periodic work (and perhaps other singleton responsibilities), rather than locking each job individually.

```java
@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 0 * * *")
public void generateStatements() {
    if (!leadership.isLeader()) return;   // only the elected leader runs it
    doGenerate();
}
```

QUARTZ CLUSTERING is the richest option. I use the Quartz scheduler (Spring Boot has a starter) configured in clustered mode with a `JDBCJobStore` on a shared database. All nodes share the Quartz tables; Quartz's row locking ensures each trigger fires on exactly one node. Beyond "run once", Quartz gives persistent jobs (schedules survive restarts), misfire handling (if all nodes were down at trigger time, it can run late or skip per policy), and rich scheduling (calendars, complex triggers). The cost is operational complexity and extra tables.

```properties
spring.quartz.job-store-type=jdbc
spring.quartz.properties.org.quartz.jobStore.isClustered=true
spring.quartz.properties.org.quartz.scheduler.instanceId=AUTO
```

Choosing between them: ShedLock for simple, in-process `@Scheduled` jobs that must run once — minimal setup, just a lock table. Quartz when I need durability, misfire handling, dynamic scheduling, or clustering as a first-class feature. Leader election when a single node should own a set of singleton responsibilities, not just one job. A senior caution for all three: the job must still be IDEMPOTENT where possible, because even "run once" mechanisms can have edge cases (a lock expiring mid-run, a leadership flip), and idempotency is the ultimate safety net. I also keep the lock/leadership store HIGHLY AVAILABLE, because if it is down the job may not run at all — I monitor and alert on both duplicate runs and missed runs.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe exactly what broke when National Bank of India scaled its batch service.

Problem 1 — statements were generated four times. The statement-generation service was deployed as four replicas for availability. The midnight `@Scheduled` cron fired on all four, so every customer received four identical statements and four notification emails. This is exactly the per-JVM scheduling problem.

Problem 2 — we needed the simplest reliable fix first. The team did not want to introduce ZooKeeper or Quartz immediately; they wanted a minimal change that guaranteed single execution. This is exactly where ShedLock fits: add a lock table and an annotation, and only one instance runs the job.

Problem 3 — a crash must not wedge the lock forever. If the winning instance crashed mid-run, the lock could block all future runs. This is exactly what `lockAtMostFor` solves: the lock auto-expires so a later trigger can proceed.

Problem 4 — even with the lock, the job had to be safe to re-run. Edge cases (lock expiry, clock skew) could theoretically cause an overlap. This is exactly the idempotency safety net: statement generation upserts by customer and period, so a duplicate attempt produces no duplicate output.

The project also records that for richer needs (persistent schedules, misfire handling) the team would move to Quartz clustering, and for owning multiple singleton tasks they would use leader election — but ShedLock was the right first fix.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `StatementJob` with a `@Scheduled` method guarded by `@SchedulerLock(name = "statementGeneration", lockAtMostFor, lockAtLeastFor)`. A ShedLock `LockProvider` is configured against a shared database `shedlock` table. The `StatementService` generates statements idempotently (upsert by customer and period). Because this chapter's tests run without a live cluster, a `SimulatedCluster` test harness models several instances racing for the lock and verifies only one wins. A test also checks the idempotent upsert. The configuration shows the lock table DDL and the ShedLock beans, with comments explaining `lockAtMostFor`/`lockAtLeastFor`, and notes Quartz/leader-election as alternatives.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the monthly statement cron firing across a four-instance cluster that shares one database.

Step 1 — all four fire. At midnight on the first of the month, the `@Scheduled` cron triggers independently inside all four JVMs, because scheduling is per-instance. Without a guard, all four would generate statements.

Step 2 — all four race for the lock. Each instance's `@SchedulerLock` tries to acquire the lock named `statementGeneration` by writing a row in the shared `shedlock` table with a `lock_until` of now plus `lockAtMostFor` (thirty minutes). The database makes this atomic: exactly one instance's write succeeds; the other three see the lock is held and their `@Scheduled` method returns immediately without running the job.

Step 3 — the winner runs. The instance that acquired the lock logs that it holds it and calls `statementService.generateForPeriod(...)`. It upserts a statement row per customer keyed by customer and period. Because the key is (customer, period), re-running would not create duplicates — the idempotency safety net.

Step 4 — safety on crash. The lock carries `lockAtMostFor = PT30M`. If the winning instance crashed mid-run, the lock would not be held forever; after thirty minutes it auto-expires in the shared table, so a future trigger (or an operator-initiated re-run) can acquire it and proceed. This prevents a wedged job.

Step 5 — safety on skew. The lock also carries `lockAtLeastFor = PT5M`, so even if the job finishes in milliseconds the lock stays held for at least five minutes. This stops a second instance, whose clock might be slightly ahead, from acquiring the just-released lock and running the job again within the same window.

Step 6 — alternatives for richer needs. The project notes that if we later needed persistent schedules, misfire handling, or dynamic scheduling, we would move to Quartz clustering with a shared JDBC job store; and if one node should own all singleton periodic work, we would use leader election. For simple run-once semantics, ShedLock was the right, minimal choice.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core problem is that a Scheduled task is local to each JVM, so when I run several replicas of a service for availability, the trigger fires inside every replica and the job runs once per instance. For a banking job that writes data, like generating statements or accruing interest, that means duplicated financial effects, which is unacceptable. There are three standard fixes. ShedLock is the lightest: I add a shared lock store, usually a small table in the same database, enable scheduler locking, and annotate the method with SchedulerLock giving it a name, a lockAtMostFor, and a lockAtLeastFor. At the trigger every instance tries to acquire the named lock atomically in the shared store; exactly one wins and runs the job, and the rest skip. Leader election makes one instance the leader so only the leader runs scheduled work, which suits a node that should own all singleton responsibilities. Quartz clustering uses the Quartz scheduler in clustered mode with a shared JDBC job store, so each trigger fires on exactly one node, and it additionally gives persistent schedules, misfire handling, and rich triggers.

The two ShedLock timers matter and interviewers probe them. lockAtMostFor is a safety expiry: if the instance holding the lock crashes mid-run, the lock auto-releases after that duration so a later trigger is not blocked forever. lockAtLeastFor is a minimum hold that guards against clock skew, so a job that finishes in milliseconds cannot be picked up and re-run by a second instance within the same window.

In our statement-batch service at National Bank of India, four replicas were each generating every customer's statement, so customers received four copies. We fixed it with ShedLock as the minimal change, guarding the monthly job with a named lock whose lockAtMostFor auto-releases a crashed holder. Crucially I kept the job idempotent, upserting statements by customer and period, because even a run-once mechanism can have edge cases around lock expiry or a leadership flip, and idempotency is the ultimate safety net. I choose ShedLock for simple run-once needs, Quartz clustering when I need persistence and misfire handling, and leader election when one node should own a whole set of periodic tasks, and in every case I monitor and alert on both duplicate runs and missed runs because a dead lock store can also prevent the job from running at all.

### 9.28 @Scheduled limitations (Q51 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: What are the limitations of Spring's @Scheduled (single-threaded default pool, no persistence of triggers, no dynamic/runtime rescheduling), and how do you work around each?
answers.shortTitle: @Scheduled limitations — single-threaded pool, no persistence, no runtime rescheduling

s1_definition.profdef: Spring's `@Scheduled` is a simple in-memory scheduler with three notable limitations. (1) SINGLE-THREADED by default: all `@Scheduled` methods share ONE thread, so a slow job blocks every other scheduled job; the fix is to configure a `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` (via `SchedulerConfigurer` or `spring.task.scheduling.pool.size`) so tasks run concurrently, or offload heavy work with `@Async`. (2) NO PERSISTENCE: triggers live only in memory, so if the app is down at the trigger time the run is simply MISSED — there is no record of jobs, no catch-up, no history; the fix is Quartz with a `JDBCJobStore` (persistent jobs and misfire handling) or an external scheduler. (3) NO RUNTIME RESCHEDULING: a `@Scheduled(cron = "...")` value is fixed at startup and cannot be changed while running; the fix is programmatic scheduling with `TaskScheduler.schedule(...)` and a `Trigger` whose cron is read dynamically, or Quartz which lets you reschedule triggers at runtime. In short, `@Scheduled` is great for simple, fixed, best-effort in-process jobs; beyond that you move to a thread pool, Quartz, or an external scheduler.
s1_definition.analogy: `@Scheduled` is like a single clerk at National Bank of India with one appointment book. Limitation one: that one clerk does one task at a time, so a long task makes everyone else wait. Limitation two: the appointment book is only in the clerk's head, so if the clerk goes home sick (the app is down) the missed appointments are simply forgotten, not rescheduled. Limitation three: the appointments are written in permanent ink at the start of the day and the clerk cannot change the time of a task on the fly. The fixes are to hire more clerks (thread pool), use a shared written diary that survives absence (Quartz persistence), and allow appointment times to be edited during the day (dynamic rescheduling).
s1_definition.oneliner: `@Scheduled` is single-threaded (one slow job blocks all — fix with a `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler`/`@Async`), has no persistence (missed while down, no history — fix with Quartz JDBC job store), and has no runtime rescheduling (cron fixed at startup — fix with programmatic `TaskScheduler` + dynamic `Trigger` or Quartz).

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe how all three limitations bit the batch service at National Bank of India.

Problem 1 — a slow reconciliation job blocked everything. Reconciliation ran for forty minutes on the single default scheduler thread, and during that time the cache-refresh and heartbeat jobs did not run at all. This is exactly the single-threaded limitation: one thread serialises every job. The fix was a `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` so the jobs run concurrently.

Problem 2 — a regulatory report was missed during a deploy. A compliance extract was scheduled for 02:00, but a deployment had the service down from 01:55 to 02:05, and the 02:00 run simply never happened — no record, no catch-up. This is exactly the no-persistence limitation. The fix recorded in the project is to move must-not-miss jobs to Quartz with a JDBC job store and a misfire policy, or to an external scheduler.

Problem 3 — business needed to move the statement run without a release. At month-end, operations wanted to shift the statement job earlier, but the cron was hard-coded and required a redeploy. This is exactly the no-runtime-rescheduling limitation. The fix is a programmatic `TaskScheduler` with a dynamic `CronTrigger` that reads the cron from a config/database value, so changing that value reschedules the job live.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. A `SchedulerConfig` registers a `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` (fixing limitation one) so multiple jobs run concurrently. A `DynamicCronService` holds the current cron in a mutable, dynamically-readable source and schedules a job programmatically with a `CronTrigger` that re-reads it (fixing limitation three), exposing a method to change the cron at runtime. The code documents (with comments and a config note) that for persistence/misfire the team uses Quartz with a JDBC job store (limitation two). A test verifies that changing the dynamic cron produces a different next execution time (proving runtime reschedule) and that the pool size allows concurrency.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the service running three scheduled jobs, plus an operator changing the statement schedule at runtime.

Step 1 — pooled scheduling (fix one). At startup, `SchedulerConfig` registers a `ThreadPoolTaskScheduler` with five threads instead of the default single thread. When the slow reconciliation job starts on thread `sched-1` and sleeps for its long work, the heartbeat job's trigger arrives and runs on `sched-2` concurrently. On the default single-thread scheduler the heartbeat would have been blocked until reconciliation finished; with the pool it runs on time.

Step 2 — missed-while-down reality (fix two). The regulatory extract is scheduled for 02:00. Because `@Scheduled` keeps triggers only in memory, if the service is down at 02:00 (a deploy or crash), the trigger never fires and nothing records or reruns it. The project documents that must-not-miss jobs belong in Quartz with a JDBC job store, which persists the job and applies a misfire policy to recover a run that was missed while the app was down.

Step 3 — dynamic scheduling setup (fix three). At startup, `DynamicCronService` schedules the statement job programmatically using the injected `TaskScheduler` and a `Trigger` whose `nextExecution` is computed from `cronProvider.currentCron()`. Crucially, the trigger RE-READS the cron value every time it computes the next fire time, so the schedule is not frozen at startup.

Step 4 — runtime reschedule. An operator calls the PUT endpoint to change the cron (for example moving the statement run to 22:00 on the last day of the month). The controller updates the `CronProvider`'s value and calls `reschedule()`, which cancels the old future and arms a new trigger. Because the trigger reads the current cron, the next fire time immediately reflects the new value — no redeploy was needed.

Step 5 — the preview confirms the change. The response returns the new cron and the computed next run time, so the operator sees the reschedule took effect. The test proves the principle by showing two different cron strings yield two different next-execution times.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring's Scheduled annotation is a simple in-memory scheduler with three limitations I keep in mind. First, it is single-threaded by default, so all scheduled methods share one thread and a single slow job blocks every other scheduled job until it finishes; I fix this by registering a ThreadPoolTaskScheduler, either through a SchedulingConfigurer bean or the pool-size property, so independent jobs run concurrently, and I keep the scheduled method quick by offloading heavy work to an async executor. Second, it has no persistence: triggers live only in the running JVM's memory, so there is no job store, no execution history, and no catch-up, which means that if the application is down at the trigger time the run is simply missed and never happens; I fix this by moving must-not-miss jobs to Quartz with a JDBC job store, which persists jobs and supports misfire handling to recover a run missed while the app was down, or to an external scheduler like a Kubernetes CronJob that invokes an endpoint. Third, it has no runtime rescheduling: the cron string is bound at startup and cannot change without a redeploy; I fix this by scheduling programmatically with a TaskScheduler and a Trigger whose cron is read dynamically from config or a database, so changing that stored value reschedules the job live, and Quartz offers the same through rescheduling a trigger.

In our batch service at National Bank of India, all three bit us. A forty-minute reconciliation job on the single default thread starved the heartbeat and cache-refresh jobs, which the thread pool fixed. A compliance extract scheduled for two in the morning was silently missed during a deployment window, which is exactly the no-persistence gap, so we moved it to Quartz with a persistent job store and a misfire policy. And operations needed to move the statement run at month-end without a release, which the dynamic cron trigger solved by letting us change the cron value at runtime.

The way I frame it to an interviewer is as an escalation ladder. The Scheduled annotation is perfect for fixed, in-process, best-effort periodic work. The moment I need concurrency I add a thread pool; the moment a job must not be missed or needs history and misfire handling I move to Quartz or an external scheduler; the moment the schedule must change at runtime I use a programmatic task scheduler with a dynamic trigger. And combined with the separate run-once-in-a-cluster concern, which I solve with ShedLock, leader election, or Quartz clustering, those decisions define a complete production scheduling strategy. Throughout, I keep jobs idempotent and observable, because any scheduler can double-fire or miss under edge conditions.

### 9.29 JPA persistence context (Q52 of 52) — FULL FORMAT

answers.question: What is the JPA persistence context — its role as the first-level cache, how it manages entities and does dirty checking, and how its scope relates to the transaction?
answers.shortTitle: JPA persistence context — first-level cache, managed entities, dirty checking, transaction scope

s1_definition.profdef: The persistence context is the set of MANAGED entity instances that an `EntityManager` tracks within a unit of work. It is the FIRST-LEVEL CACHE: within one persistence context, requesting the same entity by its id returns the SAME Java object instance — a guaranteed identity map, so repeated `find` calls for the same id hit memory, not the database. It performs DIRTY CHECKING: at load time it stores a snapshot of each managed entity's state, and at flush it compares current state against the snapshot and generates `UPDATE` SQL only for the changed fields, so you never call `save` explicitly for a managed entity. Its SCOPE in Spring is normally transaction-scoped: it is created when the `@Transactional` method begins and closed when the transaction commits or rolls back, at which point the entities become DETACHED. The persistence context also enables write-behind (SQL is batched and flushed at commit, not immediately), and it guarantees that each entity exists once per context (no duplicate instances for the same id).
s1_definition.analogy: The persistence context is like a bank clerk's working desk for one customer session. The first time the clerk fetches Rajesh's account file from the vault they keep it on the desk (first-level cache), and every further mention of that account uses the file already on the desk, not another vault trip. If the clerk pencils in a balance change on that file, they do not need a separate "please update" form — at the end of the session the clerk compares the file against the original and automatically files the one change (dirty checking). The desk is cleared when the session (transaction) ends, after which the file on the desk is just a detached photocopy.
s1_definition.oneliner: The persistence context is the EntityManager's first-level cache and identity map of managed entities; it does automatic dirty checking against a load-time snapshot and flushes changes at commit, and in Spring it is transaction-scoped — entities become detached when the transaction ends.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The persistence context is the set of MANAGED entity instances that an `EntityManager` tracks within a unit of work. It is the FIRST-LEVEL CACHE: within one persistence context, requesting the same entity by its id returns the SAME Java object instance — a guaranteed identity map, so repeated `find` calls for the same id hit memory, not the database. It performs DIRTY CHECKING: at load time it stores a snapshot of each managed entity's state, and at flush it compares current state against the snapshot and generates `UPDATE` SQL only for the changed fields, so you never call `save` explicitly for a managed entity. Its SCOPE in Spring is normally transaction-scoped: it is created when the `@Transactional` method begins and closed when the transaction commits or rolls back, at which point the entities become DETACHED. The persistence context also enables write-behind (SQL is batched and flushed at commit, not immediately), and it guarantees that each entity exists once per context (no duplicate instances for the same id).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The persistence context is like a bank clerk's working desk for one customer session. The first time the clerk fetches Rajesh's account file from the vault they keep it on the desk (first-level cache), and every further mention of that account uses the file already on the desk, not another vault trip. If the clerk pencils in a balance change on that file, they do not need a separate "please update" form — at the end of the session the clerk compares the file against the original and automatically files the one change (dirty checking). The desk is cleared when the session (transaction) ends, after which the file on the desk is just a detached photocopy.

**One line to remember:** The persistence context is the EntityManager's first-level cache and identity map of managed entities; it does automatic dirty checking against a load-time snapshot and flushes changes at commit, and in Spring it is transaction-scoped — entities become detached when the transaction ends.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me explain the persistence context carefully, because understanding it demystifies most "why did Hibernate do that?" questions.

A MANAGED entity is one currently tracked by the persistence context. You get a managed entity by loading it (`find`, a query) or by persisting a new one inside the context. While managed, the entity is under Hibernate's watch.

FIRST-LEVEL CACHE and the IDENTITY MAP. The persistence context guarantees that within one unit of work there is AT MOST ONE object instance per entity id. So if you call `em.find(Account.class, "SAV2001")` twice in the same transaction, the first call hits the database and the second returns the exact same cached instance — `==` is true. This is not a performance cache you configure; it is a correctness guarantee (an identity map) that also happens to save a query. It is scoped to the persistence context, so it does NOT survive beyond the transaction (that would be the second-level cache, a separate opt-in feature).

```java
Account a1 = em.find(Account.class, "SAV2001");   // SQL SELECT
Account a2 = em.find(Account.class, "SAV2001");   // NO SQL — same instance from the context
assert a1 == a2;                                   // identity guaranteed
```

DIRTY CHECKING. When an entity becomes managed, Hibernate takes a SNAPSHOT (a copy of its field values). At FLUSH time (before commit, or when triggered), Hibernate compares every managed entity's current state against its snapshot. If a field changed, Hibernate generates an `UPDATE` for exactly that entity. This is why you do not call `save` on a loaded entity — changing a field is enough.

```java
@Transactional
public void freeze(String id) {
    Account a = accountRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow();  // managed, snapshot taken
    a.setStatus("FROZEN");                                // just change the field
    // no save() needed — dirty checking generates UPDATE at commit
}
```

WRITE-BEHIND / FLUSH. The persistence context does not necessarily send SQL the instant you change something. It queues changes and FLUSHES them — synchronising with the database — at well-defined points: before the transaction commits, before a query that might be affected (to keep results consistent), or when you call `flush()` explicitly. This write-behind lets Hibernate batch statements and order them correctly. The default `FlushMode` is `AUTO`.

TRANSACTION SCOPE and the lifecycle states. In a typical Spring application the persistence context is TRANSACTION-SCOPED: a `@Transactional` method begins the transaction, a persistence context is created, entities loaded within it are managed, and when the method returns and the transaction commits, the context closes and those entities become DETACHED. A detached entity is a plain object Hibernate no longer tracks; changing it does nothing until you `merge` it back into a new context. The four lifecycle states (transient, managed, detached, removed) are all defined relative to the persistence context. This is also why a `LazyInitializationException` happens: touching a lazy association after the context has closed finds no session to load it.

A few senior nuances. First, a large persistence context is a memory and CPU cost, because every managed entity holds a snapshot and is dirty-checked at flush; for big read-only operations I use `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` (skips snapshots and dirty checking), DTO projections (never managed), or periodic `clear()` in batch loops. Second, the first-level cache can surprise you: a query might return stale-looking results because the identity map returns the in-context instance rather than re-reading the row; I understand this is by design. Third, `flush()` is not `commit` — flushing pushes SQL to the database within the transaction, but the transaction can still roll back. Fourth, the persistence context, not the database, is the source of truth for identity during a transaction, which is why `equals`/`hashCode` and merge semantics matter. Fifth, extended-scope persistence contexts exist (for stateful conversations) but are rare in stateless web apps; transaction scope is the norm.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe how understanding the persistence context fixed real confusion on the account service at National Bank of India.

Problem 1 — a developer called save and was surprised it was redundant. Code loaded an account, changed the balance, and called `accountRepo.save(account)`, assuming the change would otherwise be lost. In fact the entity was managed, so dirty checking would have flushed the change anyway. This is exactly the dirty-checking behaviour: a managed entity's field change is detected and flushed automatically; the explicit save was unnecessary (though harmless).

Problem 2 — two lookups of the same account returned the same object, which confused a test. A test loaded an account twice and modified one reference, expecting the other to be unaffected, but both references pointed at the same instance. This is exactly the first-level cache / identity map: within one persistence context there is one instance per id, so the second lookup returned the cached object.

Problem 3 — a change seemed to "not persist" because the method was not transactional. A change to a loaded entity was lost because the code ran outside a transaction, so there was no persistence context to manage the entity or flush the change. This is exactly the transaction-scope point: managed state and flushing require an active persistence context.

Problem 4 — a batch loop ran out of memory. A loop loaded hundreds of thousands of accounts in one transaction, and the persistence context grew unbounded with snapshots. This is exactly the large-context cost: the fix is periodic `clear()` (and readOnly for pure reads) so managed entities detach and free memory.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity. The `PersistenceContextDemoService` has methods that, each within a `@Transactional` boundary, demonstrate: the first-level cache (two finds return the same instance, one SQL), dirty checking (change a field, no explicit save, UPDATE at commit), detachment (after the transaction the entity is detached and further changes are ignored until merge), and a batch loop that periodically flushes and clears to bound the context. A test verifies identity-map behaviour and that dirty checking is what persists the change conceptually.

sections.s5_journey:
The input exercises the first-level cache and dirty checking on Rajesh's account `SAV2001`.

Step 1 — context begins. A `@Transactional` method starts, so Spring creates a persistence context bound to this transaction. Any entity loaded now will be managed within it.

Step 2 — first find hits the database. `em.find(Account.class, "SAV2001")` executes `SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001'`. Hibernate builds a managed `Account`, puts it in the persistence context's identity map keyed by id, and stores a SNAPSHOT of its field values for later dirty checking.

Step 3 — second find hits the cache. A second `em.find` for the same id does NOT run SQL. The persistence context's identity map already holds that id, so it returns the exact same instance. The two references are `==` equal — a correctness guarantee, and incidentally a saved query.

Step 4 — dirty change. In the dirty-checking method, we load the managed account and call `setBalance(950000)`. We do NOT call save. The entity is managed, so the change is simply recorded in the live object; the snapshot still holds the old balance.

Step 5 — flush and commit. As the transaction prepares to commit, Hibernate FLUSHES: it compares each managed entity's current state against its snapshot. The balance differs, so it generates `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 950000 WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001'`. This write-behind means the SQL happens at flush, not the instant we called the setter. The transaction then commits.

Step 6 — detachment. When the transactional method returns and the context closes, the `Account` becomes DETACHED. If code outside the transaction now changes a field, nothing is tracked and no SQL is generated until the entity is merged back into a new context. For a large batch, the service calls `flush()` then `clear()` periodically so managed entities detach mid-loop and their snapshots are freed, keeping memory bounded.

```
2026-10-24 01:15:30 INFO  PctxDemoService - [1st-level cache] a1 == a2 ? true (second find: no SQL)
2026-10-24 01:15:30 INFO  PctxDemoService - [dirty checking] setBalance(950000) — no save() called
2026-10-24 01:15:30 FINE  PctxDemoService - flush → compare snapshot(1000000) vs current(950000) → UPDATE
2026-10-24 01:15:30 FINE  PctxDemoService - commit → context closes → Account now DETACHED
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The persistence context is the set of managed entity instances that an EntityManager tracks within a unit of work, and it plays three roles. First, it is the first-level cache, which is really an identity map: within one persistence context there is at most one object instance per entity id, so if I load the same account by id twice in one transaction, the first call hits the database and the second returns the exact same instance with no SQL. This is a correctness guarantee, not a cache I configure, and it is scoped to the context so it does not survive the transaction. Second, it performs dirty checking: when an entity becomes managed, Hibernate takes a snapshot of its field values, and at flush time it compares the current state against that snapshot and generates an update for exactly the changed fields, which is why I never call save on a loaded entity, I just change the field. Third, it uses write-behind: changes are queued and flushed to the database at well-defined points, normally before the transaction commits, so Hibernate can batch and order the SQL.

The scope is the key to understanding entity lifecycle. In a typical Spring application the persistence context is transaction-scoped: it is created when the Transactional method begins and closed when the transaction commits or rolls back, at which point the entities become detached, and a detached entity's changes are not tracked until I merge it into a new context. This is exactly why a LazyInitializationException happens, because touching a lazy association after the context has closed finds no session to load it.

In our account service at National Bank of India, this understanding cleared up real confusion. A developer was calling save after changing a managed entity's balance, which was redundant because dirty checking would flush the change anyway. A test was surprised that two lookups of the same account returned the same object, which is simply the identity map. A change that seemed not to persist turned out to run outside a transaction, so there was no context to manage it. And a batch loop ran out of memory because the context grew unbounded with snapshots, which I fixed by periodically flushing and clearing so entities detach and free memory, and by using read-only transactions and DTO projections for pure reads so no snapshots are taken at all. The senior nuances I always mention are that a flush is not a commit, because a rollback can still undo flushed SQL, and that a large persistence context has a real memory and CPU cost, so I control its size deliberately in anything that touches many rows.

### 9.30 Session management & flush semantics (Q668-Q684 of 69)

answers.question: What is the difference between session.evict(), session.clear(), and detach()? When do you detach one entity versus all of them? How does this matter in a batch loop that runs out of memory?
answers.shortTitle: session.evict() vs session.clear() vs detach() — detach one vs all, batch loop memory

s1_definition.profdef: `session.evict(entity)` and the JPA `entityManager.detach(entity)` both remove a *single* managed entity from the persistence context, so Hibernate stops tracking it, stops dirty-checking it, and no longer holds its snapshot. `session.clear()` and `entityManager.clear()` remove *all* managed entities from the context at once. `evict` is the Hibernate `Session` method and `detach` is the JPA-standard equivalent for one entity; `clear` is the all-at-once version on both APIs. All three leave the row in the database untouched — they only change what the in-memory context tracks.

Neither action changes the actual money in the vault — it only changes which forms the officer is still actively tracking.

sections.s2_technical:
The persistence context keeps a reference to every managed entity plus a *snapshot* of its loaded state for dirty checking. That memory is the whole story here. In a long-running unit of work that loads thousands of rows, the context grows and grows, and because it holds strong references, those entities and their snapshots cannot be garbage collected until the context closes. This is the classic `OutOfMemoryError` in a naive batch job.

`entityManager.detach(account)` detaches a single entity. For example, after processing one account you can write `em.detach(account)` and Hibernate drops its reference and its snapshot, making it eligible for garbage collection. The Hibernate-native equivalent is `session.evict(account)` — functionally the same for one entity.

```java
Account rajesh = em.find(Account.class, "SAV2001");
rajesh.credit(new BigDecimal("1000"));  // still managed → will flush
em.detach(rajesh);                      // now detached → changes NOT tracked
```

Important nuance: if you `detach` an entity *before* its changes are flushed, those changes are lost, because dirty checking no longer sees it. So the safe pattern is to flush first, then clear.

`em.clear()` detaches everything at once. You call this in a batch loop after flushing a chunk: `em.flush(); em.clear();`. This writes the pending SQL to the database and then empties the context so memory is reclaimed. The Hibernate equivalent is `session.clear()`.

`detach`/`evict` for one entity is right when you want to keep most of the context but drop a specific heavy object. `clear` is right in batch processing where you process in chunks and want to reset after each chunk. A senior nuance: after `clear`, any entity you held a reference to is now detached, so touching a lazy association on it throws `LazyInitializationException`, and calling `merge` on it will issue a `SELECT` then an `UPDATE`.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — the month-end interest run crashes with OutOfMemoryError.** At National Bank of India, a nightly job credits interest to every savings account. The first version loaded all accounts, looped, and credited each one inside a single transaction. With two million accounts the JVM heap filled up and the job died. This is exactly how an unbounded persistence context behaves — every loaded Account and its snapshot stays in memory until commit.

**Problem 2 — one very large statement object hogs memory mid-loop.** While processing Rajesh's account we also loaded a huge yearly statement object we no longer need. This is exactly where detaching a *single* entity helps — we drop just that one object without disturbing the rest of the context.

What the code will do: an `InterestPostingService` that processes accounts in chunks, credits interest with BigDecimal, calls `flush()` then `clear()` every N accounts, and uses `detach` to drop a single heavy object. The demo prints context size behaviour.

Input: two million account ids, chunk size 500.

Step 1 — a lightweight JPQL query loads only the id strings, not full entities, so the first load is cheap.

Step 2 — inside the loop, `em.find` loads one Account into the context as managed, and Hibernate takes a snapshot of its fields for dirty checking.

Step 4 — after 500 accounts, `flush()` compares each managed Account to its snapshot and issues UPDATE statements to the database. The money is now written but the transaction is not committed yet.

Step 5 — `clear()` detaches all 500 accounts, dropping references and snapshots so the garbage collector can reclaim that memory. The context is empty again.

Step 6 — the loop repeats; memory stays flat instead of climbing. At the end a final `flush()` handles the last partial chunk and commit finalizes everything.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The methods `evict` and `detach` both remove a single entity from the persistence context, where `evict` is Hibernate's native Session method and `detach` is the JPA standard, while `clear` removes every managed entity at once. The crucial point is that none of them touch the database row; they only change what the in-memory context is tracking and dirty-checking. When I detach or evict an entity, Hibernate drops its reference and its snapshot, so it stops watching it for changes and the object becomes eligible for garbage collection.

The reason this matters in practice is memory. The persistence context holds a strong reference and a field snapshot for every managed entity, and in a long loop that loads thousands of rows the context grows without bound until the transaction ends, which is the classic cause of an OutOfMemoryError in a batch job. The fix is to process in chunks and call flush followed by clear after every chunk: flush pushes the buffered SQL to the database, and clear detaches everything so the heap is reclaimed before the next chunk.

At National Bank of India our month-end interest posting job originally loaded every savings account in one transaction and crashed on heap. I rewrote it to load only the ids first, then process five hundred accounts at a time, crediting interest with BigDecimal and letting dirty checking flush the updates, and after each chunk I called flush then clear so memory stayed flat in a sawtooth pattern instead of climbing. I reserve single-entity detach for the case where one particularly heavy object is no longer needed but I want to keep the rest of the context. The nuances I always mention are that detaching before a flush loses the change because dirty checking no longer sees it, and that after a clear any reference I still hold is now detached, so touching a lazy association on it throws a LazyInitializationException and a merge would re-issue a select and an update.

answers.question: What is the difference between save() and saveAndFlush() in Spring Data JPA? When would you use one over the other?
answers.shortTitle: save() vs saveAndFlush() — deferred vs immediate flush

s1_definition.profdef: `save()` on a Spring Data JPA repository makes the entity managed and schedules the INSERT or UPDATE, but it does **not** necessarily send SQL to the database immediately — the SQL is buffered and flushed at the normal flush point, usually just before the transaction commits. `saveAndFlush()` does the same persist and then **immediately** calls `flush()`, forcing Hibernate to execute the pending SQL right away within the same transaction. Both run inside the transaction and both can still be rolled back; the only difference is *when* the SQL hits the database.
s1_definition.analogy: `save()` is like handing a filled deposit slip to the teller, who puts it in the tray to process with the rest of the batch before closing the counter. `saveAndFlush()` is like asking the teller to key in that one slip right now while you wait, so you can immediately see it reflected — but the day's books still are not closed (committed) until the counter shuts.
s1_definition.oneliner: save() buffers the SQL until flush time; saveAndFlush() forces the SQL out immediately — both are still inside the transaction and can roll back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `save()` on a Spring Data JPA repository makes the entity managed and schedules the INSERT or UPDATE, but it does **not** necessarily send SQL to the database immediately — the SQL is buffered and flushed at the normal flush point, usually just before the transaction commits. `saveAndFlush()` does the same persist and then **immediately** calls `flush()`, forcing Hibernate to execute the pending SQL right away within the same transaction. Both run inside the transaction and both can still be rolled back; the only difference is *when* the SQL hits the database.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** `save()` is like handing a filled deposit slip to the teller, who puts it in the tray to process with the rest of the batch before closing the counter. `saveAndFlush()` is like asking the teller to key in that one slip right now while you wait, so you can immediately see it reflected — but the day's books still are not closed (committed) until the counter shuts.

**One line to remember:** save() buffers the SQL until flush time; saveAndFlush() forces the SQL out immediately — both are still inside the transaction and can roll back.

sections.s2_technical:
In Spring Data JPA, `save()` delegates to `EntityManager.persist()` for a new entity or `merge()` for a detached one. For a new entity, persist makes it managed and queues an INSERT in the action queue. Hibernate uses *write-behind*: it holds that SQL and sends it at the next flush, which by default happens automatically before a query that might be affected and before commit. So in the common case, calling `save()` does not produce an immediate INSERT in the SQL log.

```java
Trade t = new Trade("TRD-001", "RELIANCE", 100);
tradeRepo.save(t);     // entity managed, INSERT queued — maybe no SQL yet
// ... more work ...
// INSERT actually runs at flush/commit
```

`saveAndFlush()` calls save and then `flush()` immediately, so the INSERT or UPDATE runs right now.

```java
Trade t = new Trade("TRD-002", "TCS", 50);
tradeRepo.saveAndFlush(t);  // INSERT executes immediately, within the same TX
```

When do you actually need `saveAndFlush`? First, when you must read back something the database generates, such as a DB default, a trigger-populated column, or when a subsequent native query in the same transaction must see the row. Second, when you want a constraint violation (unique key, not-null) to surface *now* at a known line rather than later at commit where the stack trace is confusing. Third, in tests, to force the SQL and assert on it.

The senior nuances: `saveAndFlush` still does not commit, so the row is not visible to other transactions and a later exception rolls it back. Forcing a flush too often defeats Hibernate's ability to batch inserts and reorder SQL, hurting throughput in bulk operations. And for an already-managed entity, you do not need `save` at all — dirty checking handles the update — so calling `saveAndFlush` on a managed entity is only about forcing the timing of the flush.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a duplicate trade id blows up at commit with a confusing stack trace.** At National Bank of India, two trades with the same id were occasionally saved, and the unique-constraint error only appeared at commit, far from the `save()` call, making debugging painful. This is exactly where `saveAndFlush` helps — it forces the INSERT immediately so the violation surfaces right at the save line.

**Problem 2 — a reconciliation step reads trades via a native SQL query in the same transaction.** After saving a trade we immediately run a native query to reconcile, but the native query bypasses the persistence context, so it would not see the un-flushed row. This is exactly where flushing first is required.

What the code will do: a `TradeService` with one method using plain `save()` for the normal batch path and another using `saveAndFlush()` where immediate visibility or early error detection is needed. The demo logs when SQL executes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The method `save` in Spring Data JPA makes the entity managed and schedules the insert or update, but because Hibernate uses write-behind, the actual SQL is buffered and normally flushed just before the transaction commits, so calling save does not guarantee an immediate insert. The method `saveAndFlush` does exactly the same persist and then immediately calls flush, forcing Hibernate to execute the pending SQL right away. The one difference is the timing of when the SQL reaches the database; both run inside the transaction and both can still be rolled back, and neither one commits.

I default to plain save because letting Hibernate buffer lets it batch and reorder inserts, which is far better for throughput, especially in bulk operations. I reach for saveAndFlush in three specific situations. The first is when I need a constraint violation, like a duplicate primary key, to surface right at the save line with a clean stack trace instead of appearing confusingly later at commit. The second is when a later step in the same transaction reads through a path that bypasses the persistence context, such as a native SQL query, which would not see an un-flushed row. The third is in tests where I want to force the SQL and assert on the database state.

At National Bank of India our trade capture service used plain save in the normal batch path so inserts batched efficiently at commit. But we had a reconciliation method that saved a trade and then immediately ran a native SQL query to cross-check it, and that native query could not see the row until we flushed, so there I used saveAndFlush. We also had intermittent duplicate trade ids whose unique-constraint error only appeared at commit, far from the cause, so for that entry point I switched to saveAndFlush to make the violation appear at the save line. The nuances I always mention are that saveAndFlush still does not commit, so the row is invisible to other transactions and a later failure rolls it back, that flushing too aggressively defeats Hibernate's insert batching, and that for an already-managed entity I do not need save at all because dirty checking handles the update.
